input.content:
Temperature-sensitive payloads such as medicines, diagnostic samples, and perishable foods are frequently distributed in insulated containers that carry their own thermal reserve. A container of this kind is loaded at a packing point, handed to one or more carriers, and opened at a destination that may be many hours away. Because the container travels unattended and often without electrical power, the thermal behaviour of the container has to be set at the moment of closing and cannot be corrected in transit.

Two practical difficulties dominate the use of such containers. The first is the distribution of cold within the payload space. A thermal reserve placed against one wall, or laid directly on top of a payload, cools the material nearest to it strongly and the material farthest from it weakly, so the payload experiences a spread of temperatures. Direct contact between the thermal reserve and the payload can drive the contacted items below the intended range while more distant items drift above it. Moving air distributes the effect of the reserve more evenly, but a fan, pump, or other powered air mover adds a battery, a failure mode, and a service burden, and is unwelcome in a container that has to be washed, stacked, and returned.

The second difficulty is that a container which relies on an internal air path only performs as intended if that path is actually present when the container is closed. Loose internal components are lifted, rotated, or nudged during loading and during transport. If the passages that are supposed to carry conditioned air downward are displaced relative to the passages that are supposed to carry it back, the intended path is broken and the container behaves as an ordinary insulated box, without any outward sign that anything is wrong. Placing that responsibility on the person who packs the container is unreliable, because a component that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.

Related handling problems arise in reusable service. Condensate forms on cold surfaces inside a closed container and collects where it is difficult to reach. Removing it commonly means handling the thermal reserve itself, which is undesirable when the reserve is a sealed phase-change cassette that should not be opened in the field. Finally, a payload that has been briefly warmed can arrive at a temperature that appears correct, so a recipient inspecting the container at delivery cannot tell from the contents alone whether the thermal reserve lost its condition earlier in the journey.

There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier in which the internal circulation path is established positively by the act of closing the container, in which the thermal reserve is held in that established relationship during transport, and in which routine servicing and evidence of thermal exposure are available without opening the thermal reserve.

If the passages that are supposed to carry conditioned air downward are displaced relative to the passages that are supposed to carry it back, the intended path is broken and the container behaves as an ordinary insulated box, without any outward sign that anything is wrong. Placing that responsibility on the person who packs the container is unreliable, because a component that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.

+Related handling problems arise in reusable service. Condensate forms on cold surfaces inside a closed container and collects where it is difficult to reach. Removing it commonly means handling the thermal reserve itself, which is undesirable when the reserve is a sealed phase-change cassette that should not be opened in the field. Finally, a payload that has been briefly warmed can arrive at a temperature that appears correct, so a recipient inspecting the container at delivery cannot tell from the contents alone whether the thermal reserve lost its condition earlier in the journey.

+There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier in which the internal circulation path is established positively by the act of closing the container, in which the thermal reserve is held in that established relationship during transport, and in which routine servicing and evidence of thermal exposure are available without opening the thermal reserve.

A reusable passive cold-chain carrier is disclosed. The carrier includes an insulated outer shell, a removable product tray, a removable thermal module, and an insulated lid.

The removable product tray is suspended above a shell floor by tray feet so that a lower return passage remains under the removable product tray. Tray side walls of the removable product tray are spaced inward from shell side walls of the insulated outer shell to form two side supply passages. The removable product tray has perforations.

The removable thermal module includes a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes. The rigid spacer frame rests above the removable product tray and below the insulated lid. The rigid spacer frame includes a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages.

The carrier is passive and has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Warm air rising from a product region enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes, descends through the downward guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through the perforations in the removable product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The circulation path therefore surrounds the payload rather than acting on it from one side, and it is driven by the density difference that the phase-change cassettes themselves create.

The insulated lid carries a depending indexing rib. As the insulated lid closes, the depending indexing rib enters a mating channel in the rigid spacer frame and shifts the removable thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The act of closing the carrier therefore establishes the circulation path, instead of relying on the person who packs the carrier to place the removable thermal module accurately. A compressible lid gasket seals against an upper edge of the insulated outer shell after registration, so the removable thermal module is aligned before the interior is closed off. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the rigid spacer frame against ledges of the insulated outer shell so that the removable thermal module cannot lift away from the removable product tray during transport.

In some embodiments, a removable absorbent wick lies in a shallow condensate channel around the removable product tray, and condensate discharge openings at lower ends of the downward guide ducts discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel. A pull tab on the removable absorbent wick remains accessible when the removable product tray is removed, allowing the removable absorbent wick to be replaced without opening a phase-change cassette.

In some embodiments, the insulated outer shell includes a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette and retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that phase-change cassette softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette cools again and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The mechanical exposure indicator does not control airflow.

Methods are also disclosed, including a method of passively conditioning a payload in which conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the rigid spacer frame, products are placed in the removable product tray, the removable thermal module is placed above the removable product tray, and the insulated lid is closed to register and retain the removable thermal module, and a method of servicing the carrier between uses.

# FIG. 1

## View
Exploded perspective view of a reusable passive cold-chain carrier, drawn in black line work on a white background, patent drawing style with plain contour lines and no shading or colour. The four bodies are separated vertically along a common upright axis and are drawn in the same viewing direction, so that the top of each lower body is visible. Keep all line work well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

## Bodies to draw, from bottom to top

1. Insulated outer shell 10: an open-topped rectangular box seen from slightly above one front corner, with visible wall thickness. Its rim, the upper edge 16, is drawn as a narrow flat band running around the whole top of the box, distinguishable from the outer face of the box below it. The interior of the box is open and empty in this view.

2. Removable product tray 20: an open-topped rectangular pan, shorter and narrower than the shell 10, floating directly above the shell 10. Its upright walls are lower than the walls of the shell 10, and its bottom is drawn as a flat panel carrying a field of small round through holes distributed across the bottom panel.

3. Removable thermal module 40: a flat rectangular assembly, floating above the removable product tray 20 and having about the same outline in plan as the removable product tray 20. It is shown schematically as a shallow rectangular frame body of visible thickness with a single rectangular opening through its upper face at the centre, and with two upright slab-like bodies held within the frame body on opposite sides of that central opening.

4. Insulated lid 60: a rectangular slab, floating above the removable thermal module 40 and matching the outline of the shell 10 in plan. The lid 60 is tipped in the same perspective as the other bodies so that its underside is visible. On the underside, a compressible lid gasket 64 is drawn as a continuous band set in from the perimeter of the underside and running all the way around it.

5. Mechanical exposure indicator 80: a small raised housing on the outer face of one visible upright wall of the shell 10, near the upper part of that wall, drawn schematically as a small rectangular boss standing proud of the wall face.

## Relationships that must read from the drawing
- The removable product tray 20, the removable thermal module 40, and the insulated lid 60 are each smaller than or equal in plan to the opening of the shell 10, and are aligned one above the other so that they would descend into or onto the shell 10.
- The upper edge 16 lies at the top of the shell 10, facing the compressible lid gasket 64 on the underside of the insulated lid 60.
- The mechanical exposure indicator 80 is on the outside of the shell 10.

10, 16, 20, 40, 60, 64, 80

In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright attitude of use, in which the insulated lid is uppermost. The described embodiments illustrate the invention and do not limit it.

## Overview of the carrier

Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, a reusable passive cold-chain carrier includes an insulated outer shell 10, a removable product tray 20, a removable thermal module 40, and an insulated lid 60. The insulated outer shell 10 has a shell floor 12, shell side walls 14 rising from the shell floor 12, and an upper edge 16 at the top of the shell side walls 14. The insulated outer shell 10, the insulated lid 60, and the walls that bound the interior are of insulating construction, for example a rigid foam core within a washable outer skin, so that the carrier can be cleaned, stacked, and returned for reuse.

The removable product tray 20 receives the payload. The removable product tray 20 has a bottom, tray side walls 24, and tray feet 22 depending from the bottom. The tray feet 22 stand on the shell floor 12 and suspend the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12, so that a lower return passage 28 remains under the removable product tray 20. The tray feet 22 are spaced apart from one another so that the lower return passage 28 is continuous beneath the removable product tray 20 from one side of the insulated outer shell 10 to the other. The tray side walls 24 are spaced inward from the shell side walls 14 to form two side supply passages 30, each side supply passage 30 extending upward from the lower return passage 28 alongside the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through its bottom, distributed across the bottom, so that the interior of the removable product tray 20 communicates with the lower return passage 28.

The removable product tray 20 lifts out of the insulated outer shell 10 as a unit, with the payload in it, once the removable thermal module 40 has been taken out. Loading and unloading therefore do not disturb the passages, because the passages are formed by the position that the removable product tray 20 takes up when it is returned to the insulated outer shell 10 and not by any separate ducting that has to be assembled.

## The removable thermal module

Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 3, the removable thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 holding two opposed phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 is a self-supporting frame body, for example of moulded polymer, stiff enough that the phase-change cassettes 44 it carries do not close the passages formed in it. The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.

The rigid spacer frame 42 includes a central inlet opening 46 through its upper region, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the phase-change cassettes 44, and peripheral outlet openings 50. Each phase-change cassette 44 is a sealed cassette of phase-change material that is conditioned before use, and the two phase-change cassettes 44 are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening 46 with their faces mutually opposed. Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44 and opens at its lower end. The peripheral outlet openings 50 lie at the periphery of the rigid spacer frame 42 and are aligned with the side supply passages 30 when the removable thermal module 40 is in a registered position.

Because the two phase-change cassettes 44 are opposed and are held apart by the rigid spacer frame 42, the air that enters between them is exposed to two cooled faces at once, and no face of the payload is in contact with a phase-change cassette 44. The payload is conditioned by the air that has passed the phase-change cassettes 44, rather than by conduction into a cassette lying on top of it.

## The registered passive circulation path

The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow.

In use, warm air rising from a product region within the removable product tray 20 enters the central inlet opening 46, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, descends through the downward guide ducts 48, enters the side supply passages 30, passes through the perforations 26 in the removable product tray 20, and returns through the lower return passage 28 to the product region. The path is closed on itself and surrounds the removable product tray 20 on the sides and underneath, so that cooled air is delivered to the payload from below and around it and warmed air is drawn off from above it.

The path exists only when the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. If the removable thermal module 40 is set down out of position, the peripheral outlet openings 50 discharge against the tray side walls 24 or against the shell side walls 14, the descending limb of the path is blocked, and the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box. This is the failure that the registration described below is directed to, and it is a failure that gives no outward sign, because a removable thermal module 40 that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.

## Lid-driven registration and retention

Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 3, the insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62, and the rigid spacer frame 42 has a mating channel 52 that receives the depending indexing rib 62. As the insulated lid 60 closes, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 52 and shifts the removable thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. The registration is therefore performed by the act of closing the carrier. The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position.

The depending indexing rib 62 and the mating channel 52 are shaped so that the rib meets the channel over a range of initial positions of the removable thermal module 40 and draws it inward as the insulated lid 60 descends, the last part of the closing movement bringing the removable thermal module 40 fully into the registered position. In some embodiments the depending indexing rib 62 and the mating channel 52 are elongate and asymmetrically placed on the rigid spacer frame 42, so that the removable thermal module 40 can be seated in only one orientation and the peripheral outlet openings 50 cannot be presented to the wrong side of the interior.

A compressible lid gasket 64 on the insulated lid 60 seals against the upper edge 16 of the insulated outer shell 10 after registration. The order of these two events matters. The depending indexing rib 62 engages the mating channel 52 and completes the registration while the compressible lid gasket 64 is still clear of the upper edge 16, so that the removable thermal module 40 is free to be shifted by the depending indexing rib 62 and is not being asked to move after the interior has been closed off. Only then does continued closing compress the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 and seal the interior.

The same closing movement presses resilient feet 54 of the rigid spacer frame 42 against ledges 18 of the insulated outer shell 10, so that the removable thermal module 40 cannot lift away from the removable product tray 20 during transport. The ledges 18 project inward from the shell side walls 14 at the level at which the removable thermal module 40 is seated. The resilient feet 54 are compliant limbs of the rigid spacer frame 42, and the closing insulated lid 60 deflects them against the ledges 18 so that they remain loaded while the carrier is closed. The load holds the removable thermal module 40 down against handling, tilting, and vibration in transit, which would otherwise let the removable thermal module 40 rise and break the overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 50 and the side supply passages 30. When the insulated lid 60 is opened, the resilient feet 54 relax and the removable thermal module 40 lifts out by hand without a tool.

Registration and retention are thus produced by the same movement that a user has to make in any event. Nothing has to be latched, clamped, or checked separately, and there is no state in which the carrier is closed and sealed but the circulation path is not established.

## Condensate handling and the removable wick

Referring to FIG. 4, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing on the shell floor 12.

The removable absorbent wick 72 has a pull tab 74. The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44 and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40. Routine servicing between journeys therefore does not require handling of the sealed phase-change cassettes 44, which are conditioned items that should be returned to conditioning intact. In some embodiments the removable absorbent wick 72 is a strip of absorbent material sized to the length of the shallow condensate channel 70, and the pull tab 74 is an extension of that strip at one end that stands above the rim of the shallow condensate channel 70.

## Mechanical exposure indicator

Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, the insulated outer shell 10 includes a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside. An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. A spring 86 acts on the indicator stem 82 in the outward direction and is held by the temperature-responsive latch 84 while the phase-change cassette 44 remains in condition.

If that phase-change cassette 44 softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch 84, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette 44 cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The value of this behaviour is that a payload which was warmed part way through a journey and then cooled again arrives at a temperature that looks correct, and the contents alone give the recipient no way to know what happened. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 records the event in the structure of the carrier and holds the record until a person opens the carrier and deliberately resets it.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. The interior of the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is separate from the circulation path, and the circulation path is the same whether the indicator stem 82 is retained or has moved to the latched exposed position. The thermal condition being reported is taken directly from a phase-change cassette 44, that is, from the reserve that actually conditions the payload, and no electrical power, battery, or logging device is required for the indication.

## Method of passively conditioning a payload

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes 44 are fitted to the rigid spacer frame 42 to form the removable thermal module 40, products are placed in the removable product tray 20, the removable product tray 20 is placed in the insulated outer shell 10 on its tray feet 22, the removable thermal module 40 is placed above the removable product tray 20, and the insulated lid 60 is closed. Closing the insulated lid 60 brings the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 52, shifts the removable thermal module 40 into the registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30, presses the resilient feet 54 against the ledges 18, and then compresses the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16. Air then circulates passively along the path described above for the duration of the journey.

At the destination the insulated lid 60 is opened, the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out, and the removable product tray 20 is lifted out with the payload in it. Between journeys the removable absorbent wick 72 is withdrawn from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and replaced, the interior is cleaned, the phase-change cassettes 44 are returned for conditioning, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset by hand if it has moved to the latched exposed position.

## Variations

The number of perforations 26 and their distribution across the bottom of the removable product tray 20 are chosen for the payload being carried, a wider distribution giving a more even delivery from the side supply passages 30 into the interior of the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 may be provided in more than one depth for the same insulated outer shell 10, the tray feet 22 in each case suspending the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12 so that the lower return passage 28 remains. The phase-change cassettes 44 may be exchanged for cassettes of a different phase-change material to suit a different transport range, without any change to the rigid spacer frame 42, the depending indexing rib 62, or the mating channel 52, because registration is a matter of the frame geometry and not of the cassettes.

The removable absorbent wick 72 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features. A carrier may be built with the registered passive circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with either optional feature separately, or with both. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another where the combination is physically consistent.

This is the failure that the registration described below is directed to, and it is a failure that gives no outward sign, because a removable thermal module 40 that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.

## Lid-driven registration and retention

Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 3, the insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62, and the rigid spacer frame 42 has a mating channel 52 that receives the depending indexing rib 62. As the insulated lid 60 closes, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 52 and shifts the removable thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. The registration is therefore performed by the act of closing the carrier. The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position.

The depending indexing rib 62 and the mating channel 52 are shaped so that the rib meets the channel over a range of initial positions of the removable thermal module 40 and draws it inward as the insulated lid 60 descends, the last part of the closing movement bringing the removable thermal module 40 fully into the registered position. In some embodiments the depending indexing rib 62 and the mating channel 52 are elongate and asymmetrically placed on the rigid spacer frame 42, so that the removable thermal module 40 can be seated in only one orientation and the peripheral outlet openings 50 cannot be presented to the wrong side of the interior.

A compressible lid gasket 64 on the insulated lid 60 seals against the upper edge 16 of the insulated outer shell 10 after registration. The order of these two events matters. The depending indexing rib 62 engages the mating channel 52 and completes the registration while the compressible lid gasket 64 is still clear of the upper edge 16, so that the removable thermal module 40 is free to be shifted by the depending indexing rib 62 and is not being asked to move after the interior has been closed off. Only then does continued closing compress the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 and seal the interior.

The same closing movement presses resilient feet 54 of the rigid spacer frame 42 against ledges 18 of the insulated outer shell 10, so that the removable thermal module 40 cannot lift away from the removable product tray 20 during transport. The ledges 18 project inward from the shell side walls 14 at the level at which the removable thermal module 40 is seated. The resilient feet 54 are compliant limbs of the rigid spacer frame 42, and the closing insulated lid 60 deflects them against the ledges 18 so that they remain loaded while the carrier is closed. The load holds the removable thermal module 40 down against handling, tilting, and vibration in transit, which would otherwise let the removable thermal module 40 rise and break the overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 50 and the side supply passages 30. When the insulated lid 60 is opened, the resilient feet 54 relax and the removable thermal module 40 lifts out by hand without a tool.

## Condensate handling and the removable wick

Referring to FIG. 4, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing on the shell floor 12.

The removable absorbent wick 72 has a pull tab 74. The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44 and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40. Routine servicing between journeys therefore does not require handling of the sealed phase-change cassettes 44, which are conditioned items that should be returned to conditioning intact. In some embodiments the removable absorbent wick 72 is a strip of absorbent material sized to the length of the shallow condensate channel 70, and the pull tab 74 is an extension of that strip at one end that stands above the rim of the shallow condensate channel 70.

## Mechanical exposure indicator

Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, the insulated outer shell 10 includes a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside. An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. A spring 86 acts on the indicator stem 82 in the outward direction and is held by the temperature-responsive latch 84 while the phase-change cassette 44 remains in condition.

If that phase-change cassette 44 softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch 84, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette 44 cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The value of this behaviour is that a payload which was warmed part way through a journey and then cooled again arrives at a temperature that looks correct, and the contents alone give the recipient no way to know what happened. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 records the event in the structure of the carrier and holds the record until a person opens the carrier and deliberately resets it.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. The interior of the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is separate from the circulation path, and the circulation path is the same whether the indicator stem 82 is retained or has moved to the latched exposed position. The thermal condition being reported is taken directly from a phase-change cassette 44, that is, from the reserve that actually conditions the payload, and no electrical power, battery, or logging device is required for the indication.

## Method of passively conditioning a payload

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes 44 are fitted to the rigid spacer frame 42 to form the removable thermal module 40, products are placed in the removable product tray 20, the removable product tray 20 is placed in the insulated outer shell 10 on its tray feet 22, the removable thermal module 40 is placed above the removable product tray 20, and the insulated lid 60 is closed. Closing the insulated lid 60 brings the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 52, shifts the removable thermal module 40 into the registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30, presses the resilient feet 54 against the ledges 18, and then compresses the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16. Air then circulates passively along the path described above for the duration of the journey.

At the destination the insulated lid 60 is opened, the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out, and the removable product tray 20 is lifted out with the payload in it. Between journeys the removable absorbent wick 72 is withdrawn from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and replaced, the interior is cleaned, the phase-change cassettes 44 are returned for conditioning, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset by hand if it has moved to the latched exposed position.

## Variations

The number of perforations 26 and their distribution across the bottom of the removable product tray 20 are chosen for the payload being carried, a wider distribution giving a more even delivery from the side supply passages 30 into the interior of the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 may be provided in more than one depth for the same insulated outer shell 10, the tray feet 22 in each case suspending the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12 so that the lower return passage 28 remains. The phase-change cassettes 44 may be exchanged for cassettes of a different phase-change material to suit a different transport range, without any change to the rigid spacer frame 42, the depending indexing rib 62, or the mating channel 52, because registration is a matter of the frame geometry and not of the cassettes.

The removable absorbent wick 72 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features. A carrier may be built with the registered passive circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with either optional feature separately, or with both. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another where the combination is physically consistent.

a removable product tray within the insulated outer shell, the removable product tray having a bottom with perforations through the bottom, tray side walls, and tray feet suspending the removable product tray above the shell floor so that a lower return passage remains under the removable product tray, the tray side walls being spaced inward from the shell side walls to form two side supply passages, each side supply passage extending upward from the lower return passage alongside the removable product tray;

a removable thermal module comprising a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes, the rigid spacer frame resting above the removable product tray and including a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings; and

an insulated lid above the removable thermal module and carrying a depending indexing rib, the rigid spacer frame having a mating channel that receives the depending indexing rib as the insulated lid closes, whereby the depending indexing rib shifts the removable thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages;

wherein the carrier has no fan, pump, or powered air mover, and wherein, in the registered position, the central inlet opening, faces of the phase-change cassettes, the downward guide ducts, the peripheral outlet openings, the side supply passages, the perforations, and the lower return passage define a circulation path that is closed on itself and along which air rising from a product region within the removable product tray returns to the product region.

2. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a compressible lid gasket that seals against the upper edge of the insulated outer shell after registration, the depending indexing rib engaging the mating channel while the compressible lid gasket is clear of the upper edge, and continued closing of the insulated lid thereafter compressing the compressible lid gasket against the upper edge.

3. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the rigid spacer frame has resilient feet and the insulated outer shell has ledges, and closing of the insulated lid presses the resilient feet against the ledges so that the removable thermal module cannot lift away from the removable product tray during transport.

4. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 3, wherein the ledges project inward from the shell side walls at a level at which the removable thermal module is seated, and the resilient feet are compliant limbs of the rigid spacer frame that remain loaded against the ledges while the carrier is closed and relax when the insulated lid is opened.

5. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the depending indexing rib and the mating channel are elongate and asymmetrically placed on the rigid spacer frame, so that the removable thermal module is seated in only one orientation.

6. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the two phase-change cassettes are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening with faces of the phase-change cassettes mutually opposed, and each downward guide duct extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes and opens at a lower end of that downward guide duct.

7. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the tray feet are spaced apart from one another so that the lower return passage is continuous beneath the removable product tray from one side of the insulated outer shell to the other, and the perforations are distributed across the bottom of the removable product tray.

8. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the removable thermal module lifts out of the insulated outer shell as one piece with both phase-change cassettes, and the removable product tray thereafter lifts out of the insulated outer shell with a payload in it.

9. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a shallow condensate channel extending around the removable product tray, wherein condensate discharge openings at lower ends of the downward guide ducts discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel.

10. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 9, further comprising a removable absorbent wick lying in the shallow condensate channel.

11. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 10, wherein the removable absorbent wick has a pull tab that remains accessible when the removable product tray is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick is replaced without opening a phase-change cassette.

12. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the insulated outer shell includes a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside, the mechanical exposure indicator comprising an indicator stem thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette, a temperature-responsive latch retaining the indicator stem, and a spring that moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position when that phase-change cassette softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch.

13. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 12, wherein the indicator stem remains in the latched exposed position after that phase-change cassette cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened.

14. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 12, wherein the mechanical exposure indicator does not control airflow, an interior of the mechanical exposure indicator being separate from the circulation path and the circulation path being the same whether the indicator stem is retained by the temperature-responsive latch or has moved to the latched exposed position.

15. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the phase-change cassettes are exchangeable for cassettes of a different phase-change material without change to the rigid spacer frame, the depending indexing rib, or the mating channel.

16. A method of passively conditioning a payload, comprising:

fitting two conditioned phase-change cassettes to a rigid spacer frame to form a removable thermal module, the rigid spacer frame including a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings;

placing products in a removable product tray;

placing the removable product tray in an insulated outer shell on tray feet that suspend the removable product tray above a shell floor of the insulated outer shell so that a lower return passage remains under the removable product tray, tray side walls of the removable product tray being spaced inward from shell side walls of the insulated outer shell to form two side supply passages;

placing the removable thermal module above the removable product tray;

closing an insulated lid onto the insulated outer shell so that a depending indexing rib carried by the insulated lid enters a mating channel of the rigid spacer frame and shifts the removable thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages; and

thereafter circulating air passively, without a fan, pump, or powered air mover, from a product region within the removable product tray into the central inlet opening, along faces of the phase-change cassettes, downward through the downward guide ducts, through the peripheral outlet openings into the side supply passages, through perforations in the removable product tray, and back to the product region through the lower return passage.

17. The method of claim 16, wherein closing the insulated lid registers the removable thermal module before a compressible lid gasket carried by the insulated lid seals against an upper edge of the insulated outer shell, and continued closing thereafter compresses the compressible lid gasket against the upper edge.

18. The method of claim 16, wherein closing the insulated lid presses resilient feet of the rigid spacer frame against ledges of the insulated outer shell so that the removable thermal module cannot lift away from the removable product tray during transport.

19. The method of claim 16, further comprising, at a destination, opening the insulated lid, lifting the removable thermal module out of the insulated outer shell as one piece with both phase-change cassettes, and thereafter lifting the removable product tray out of the insulated outer shell with the payload in it.

20. A method of servicing a passive cold-chain carrier between uses, comprising:

opening an insulated lid of the carrier and withdrawing a depending indexing rib carried by the insulated lid from a mating channel of a rigid spacer frame of a removable thermal module, the rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes and having two downward guide ducts beside the phase-change cassettes;

lifting the removable thermal module out of an insulated outer shell of the carrier;

lifting a removable product tray out of the insulated outer shell, thereby exposing a pull tab of a removable absorbent wick lying in a shallow condensate channel that extends around the removable product tray and that receives condensate from condensate discharge openings at lower ends of the downward guide ducts;

withdrawing the removable absorbent wick from the shallow condensate channel by the pull tab and placing a replacement absorbent wick in the shallow condensate channel, without opening a phase-change cassette; and

returning the removable product tray and the removable thermal module to the insulated outer shell and closing the insulated lid so that the depending indexing rib enters the mating channel and shifts the removable thermal module into a registered position in which peripheral outlet openings of the rigid spacer frame overlap side supply passages formed between tray side walls of the removable product tray and shell side walls of the insulated outer shell.

21. The method of claim 20, further comprising resetting by hand a mechanical exposure indicator of the insulated outer shell from a latched exposed position to which a spring moved an indicator stem of the mechanical exposure indicator when a phase-change cassette thermally coupled to the indicator stem softened enough to release a temperature-responsive latch.

input.content: A reusable passive cold-chain carrier has an insulated outer shell, a removable product tray, a removable thermal module, and an insulated lid. Tray feet suspend the product tray above the shell floor to leave a lower return passage, and the tray side walls are spaced inward from the shell side walls to form two side supply passages. The thermal module is a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes and having a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings. As the lid closes, a depending indexing rib on the lid enters a mating channel in the spacer frame and shifts the module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, and a lid gasket then seals against the upper edge of the shell. Without any fan, pump, or powered air mover, air rising from the product region enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts into the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage.

# FIG. 1

## View
Exploded perspective view of a reusable passive cold-chain carrier, in black line work on a white background, patent drawing style, no shading or colour. The four bodies are separated vertically along a common upright axis and drawn in the same viewing direction, seen from slightly above one front corner so the top of each lower body is visible. Keep all line work well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

## Bodies, from bottom to top
- Insulated outer shell 10: an open-topped rectangular box with visible wall thickness, its interior open and empty in this view. Its rim, the upper edge 16, is a narrow flat band running around the whole top of the box, distinguishable from the outer face below it.
- Removable product tray 20: an open-topped rectangular pan, smaller in plan than the shell 10 and with lower walls, floating directly above the shell 10. Its bottom is a flat panel carrying a field of small round through holes distributed across the panel.
- Removable thermal module 40: a flat rectangular assembly floating above the tray 20 and about the same outline in plan, shown schematically as a shallow rectangular frame body of visible thickness with one rectangular opening through its upper face at the centre, and two upright slab-like bodies held within the frame body on opposite sides of that opening.
- Insulated lid 60: a rectangular slab floating above the module 40, matching the shell 10 in plan, tipped in the same perspective so that its underside is visible. A compressible lid gasket 64 is drawn on that underside as a continuous band set in from the perimeter and running all the way around it.
- Mechanical exposure indicator 80: a small rectangular boss standing proud of the outer face of one visible upright wall of the shell 10, in the upper part of that wall.

## Relationships
- The tray 20, the module 40, and the lid 60 are each smaller than or equal in plan to the opening of the shell 10 and are aligned one above the other, so that they would descend into or onto the shell 10.
- The upper edge 16 faces the compressible lid gasket 64.
- The mechanical exposure indicator 80 is on the outside of the shell 10.

## Reference numerals appearing on this sheet
10, 16, 20, 40, 60, 64, 80

Enlarged schematic vertical sectional view of one lateral region of the carrier, on an upright plane cutting from side to side, in black line work on a white background, patent drawing style. The view runs from the lower part of the thermal module at the top of the drawing area down to the bottom of the carrier interior. Sectioned solids carry uniform diagonal hatching; open spaces are blank. Keep all line work well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

## Context bodies, drawn without numerals
An upright hatched slab of substantial thickness stands at the outboard side over the full height of the view. A horizontal hatched slab of substantial thickness runs along the bottom and meets that upright slab. A hatched frame body occupies the upper part of the view.

## Bodies and spaces
- Downward guide duct 48: a blank open upright passage in the upper part of the view, bounded on each side by a web of the frame body and ending at the lower edge of that frame body.
- Peripheral outlet opening 50: a gap through the outboard web bounding the duct 48, opening sideways from the duct 48 toward the upright outboard slab.
- Condensate discharge opening 56: a gap at the lower end of the duct 48, through the lower web of the frame body, opening downward.
- Tray side wall 24: an upright hatched panel of modest thickness in the lower part of the view, inboard of and spaced from the upright outboard slab so that a blank open gap runs upward between them. Its lower end joins a horizontal hatched bottom panel extending to the inboard edge of the view.
- Tray foot 22: a short hatched support between the underside of that bottom panel and the upper surface of the horizontal bottom slab, with blank open space to each side of it.
- Shallow condensate channel 70: a shallow upwardly open trough in the upper surface of the horizontal bottom slab, between the foot of the upright outboard slab and the lower end of the wall 24, its depth small compared with its width, lying below the opening 56.
- Removable absorbent wick 72: an elongate body lying in the trough of the channel 70 and following its floor, hatched in a pattern distinct from the surrounding solids, occupying most of the width of the trough and standing lower than its rim.
- Pull tab 74: a short narrow tongue continuous with the inboard end of the wick 72, rising out of the channel 70 above the rim of the trough and clear of the wall 24.

## Relationships
- The duct 48 opens sideways through the opening 50 into the upright gap alongside the wall 24, and downward through the opening 56 toward the channel 70.
- That upright gap is continuous downward with the open space above the horizontal bottom slab beside the foot 22.
- The pull tab 74 is reachable from above.

# FIG. 3

## View
Enlarged schematic vertical sectional view of an upper region of the carrier in the closed condition, on an upright plane cutting from side to side, in black line work on a white background, patent drawing style. Sectioned solids carry uniform diagonal hatching; open spaces are blank. Keep all line work well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

## Context bodies, drawn without numerals
A horizontal hatched slab of substantial thickness spans the top of the view. An upright hatched slab of substantial thickness stands at each side, rising to meet that top slab.

## Bodies
- Ledge 18: an inwardly projecting step on the inward-facing surface of each upright side slab, drawn as a short horizontal shelf surface, the slab being thicker below the step than above it.
- Rigid spacer frame 42: a hatched frame body of visible wall thickness occupying the width between the two upright side slabs and lying below the top slab, drawn as an upper horizontal web, two outboard upright webs, and short lower web portions, all continuous with one another.
- Central inlet opening 46: one rectangular gap through the upper web of the frame 42, at the centre of the width, open upward toward the top slab and downward into the interior of the frame 42.
- Phase-change cassette 44: two upright slab-like bodies of equal size held within the frame 42, one on each side of the opening 46, each with its own outline and its own hatching pattern distinct from that of the frame 42. They face one another across a blank open space lying directly below the opening 46, and each has an outboard surface facing the nearer outboard web of the frame 42.
- Downward guide duct 48: two blank open upright passages, one on each side, each between the outboard surface of one cassette 44 and the nearer outboard web of the frame 42, each open at its lower end at the bottom of the view.
- Mating channel 52: an upwardly open recess in the upper web of the frame 42, to one side of the opening 46 and bounded on both sides by hatched material of the frame 42.
- Depending indexing rib 62: a downwardly projecting hatched tongue integral with the underside of the top slab, aligned above the mating channel 52 and entering it, its side surfaces facing those of the channel 52 across a narrow blank clearance.
- Resilient foot 54: a downwardly projecting hatched limb of reduced thickness at each outboard lower corner of the frame 42, bearing downward onto and in contact with the shelf surface of the adjacent ledge 18.

## Relationships
- The space between the two cassettes 44 is continuous with the opening 46 above it and with both ducts 48 around the lower parts of the cassettes 44.
- The rib 62 and the channel 52 are engaged, and both feet 54 are seated on the ledges 18 at the same time.

## Reference numerals appearing on this sheet
18, 42, 44, 46, 48, 52, 54, 62

lines: ## Condensate handling and the removable wick

-Referring to FIG. 4, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing in the bottom of the interior.

+Referring to FIG. 2 and FIG. 4, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing in the bottom of the interior.

The removable absorbent wick 72 has a pull tab 74. The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44 and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40. Routine servicing between journeys therefore does not require handling of the sealed phase-change cassettes 44, which are conditioned items that should be returned to conditioning intact. In some embodiments the removable absorbent wick 72 is a strip of absorbent material sized to the length of the shallow condensate channel 70, and the pull tab 74 is an extension of that strip at one end that stands above the rim of the shallow condensate channel 70.

input.summary: Wrote the complete first draft of the V36 passive cold-chain carrier application: all ten sections in draft/, a 30-entry numeral table, and five figure specifications (exploded perspective, full vertical section showing the circulation circuit, enlarged section of the spacer frame with lid rib engaged, enlarged lateral section with the condensate channel and wick, and enlarged section of the mechanical exposure indicator). Claim 1 is an apparatus claim built on the registered passive circulation path plus lid-driven registration; there are two further independent claims (a method of passively conditioning a payload and a method of servicing between uses) and eighteen dependent claims forming a graduated ladder. Note plainly: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the prior_art directory contains no reference files, so no prior-art search was available to this draft and no citations appear anywhere in it. The art you were given may be incomplete, and claim scope was set from the disclosure alone; a search should be run before filing and claim 1 revisited against whatever it returns.
reasoning: Claim 1 carries two features together that do the real technical work of the invention: the peripheral outlet openings of the spacer frame must overlap the side supply passages for the path to exist, and that overlap is produced by the closing lid, whose depending indexing rib enters the mating channel and shifts the module into the registered position. An insulated box with a coolant plate above the payload, or even one with a deliberate convection gap, does not have a lid feature that mechanically positions a removable thermal module so that its outlets line up with the shell-to-tray gaps. That coupling of closing motion to path completion, not the passive convection itself, is what claim 1 is built around.

I kept the negative recitation that the carrier has no fan, pump, or powered air mover in claim 1 even though it narrows scope. The disclosure states it as a characteristic of the carrier, and it distinguishes the whole family of air-circulating shippers that solve the distribution problem with a blower. Without it, claim 1 would read on a powered unit that happens to have an indexing rib.

Left out of claim 1 deliberately: the compressible lid gasket, the resilient feet and ledges, the asymmetric rib and channel, the condensate channel, the wick and pull tab, and the whole exposure indicator. None of them is needed for the registered path to be established or to work, so each is scope that would have been given away for nothing. They are claims 2, 3 and 4, 5, 9, 10 and 11, and 12 through 14 respectively, ordered so the nearest fallbacks (gasket ordering, then retention against lift) come first.

The sequencing limitation in claim 2 is written as an ordering of events during a single closing movement, that is, registration completes while the gasket is still clear of the upper edge and only then does the gasket compress. That is a fallback that is genuinely arguable on its own, because it explains why the module can still be moved when the rib acts on it, and the description carries the same explanation in the same words.

Claim 14 recites that the exposure indicator does not control airflow and that the circulation path is identical in both indicator states. The disclosure says the indicator does not control airflow, and stating it positively in a dependent claim forecloses an argument that the carrier is really a thermally actuated damper, which is a different device with its own art.

Three statutory routes were written because they are infringed by different parties: the carrier itself (claims 1 to 15), the packing operation (claims 16 to 19), and the reconditioning depot operation (claims 20 and 21). Claim 20 is drafted as a standalone service method reciting only the structure it needs, so it survives independently if the apparatus claim is amended, and it captures the wick replacement without opening a cassette, which is a distinct commercial act.

The description was widened beyond a restatement of the disclosure in exactly two places, both to support claim language rather than to add invention. The draft is complete and filing-clean.

**Body text.** All ten sections in `draft/` are written. The Background sets up four problems the invention addresses: uneven cold distribution when a thermal reserve acts from one side, the service cost of a powered air mover in a reusable carrier, the silent failure of an internal air path whose passages are not aligned when the box is closed, and condensate and transient-warming evidence that today require handling the sealed reserve. The Detailed Description then carries every claim limitation in the same words, including the two passages a later prosecution argument would be built from: why a misplaced module silently defeats the path, and why registration must complete before the gasket seals.

**Claims.** 21 claims in three statutory routes. Claim 1 recites the carrier with the tray suspended on feet over a lower return passage, tray walls spaced inward to form two side supply passages, a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes with a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts and peripheral outlet openings, and a lid whose depending indexing rib enters a mating channel to shift the module into a registered position in which the outlets overlap the side supply passages, the whole having no fan, pump, or powered air mover and defining a circulation path closed on itself. Claim 16 is the packing method, claim 20 the depot servicing method. Dependents 2 to 15 run from the nearest fallbacks (gasket ordering, lid-loaded retention) out to genuinely separate embodiments (wick chain, irreversible indicator chain).

**Drawings.** Five sheets in `figures/`, each self-contained and each listing eight numerals or fewer: exploded perspective; full vertical section showing the closed circuit around the tray; enlarged upper-region section with the rib in the channel and the resilient feet on the ledges; enlarged lateral section with the outlet opening, condensate discharge, channel, wick, and pull tab; and enlarged section of the exposure indicator. `draft/numerals.md` holds 30 numerals, each used in the description and each appearing on at least one sheet.

The art you were given may be incomplete. Claim 1 was written from the disclosure alone, around the lid-driven registration of the module into path-completing alignment, which is the feature least likely to be met by ordinary passive shipper art. Run a search and re-test claim 1 against the results; the dependent ladder was deliberately built so that a narrowing amendment has somewhere worth retreating to.

The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

# Previous review - verdict: fail

The draft is a faithful, well-organised rendering of the inventor's disclosure at the level of the core invention (shell/tray/module/lid, the registered passive circulation loop, lid-driven registration and retention, the wick, and the irreversible exposure indicator), and the abstract now sits at 140 words, clearing the previous filing gate. Three classes of defect remain. First, no drawing sheets exist at all: figures/ contains five Markdown briefs and no rendered-*.png, and there is no review/figure-audit-evidence.json, so all five described figures and all thirty specification numerals are unillustrated - this is the root cause of both mechanical failures. Second, several structural, material, dimensional and variant details in the description, figure briefs and claims are not traceable to input/disclosure.md or input/conversation.md (the disclosure and the conversation are word-for-word identical, so there is no second source): notably the perforations being "through its bottom", the elongate/asymmetric keying of rib and channel in claim 5, the interchangeable-cassette variant of claim 15 and the multi-depth tray, the foam-core/moulded-polymer materials, the wick's strip geometry, and the ledge/foot specifics in claim 4. Third, the added "bottom" perforation limitation creates a self-contradiction in the recited flow path, which is stated in both directions within a single paragraph and again in claims 1 and 16. No [REF:...] citations appear in the draft and prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to check under citation fidelity; as the drafting brief notes, no prior-art search was run and the available art is empty rather than merely incomplete.

No text, numeral definition, or part need be removed or added to satisfy the check.
- **[critical] Perforations located "through its bottom" and "distributed across the bottom" are not in the disclosure** (draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶7 and ¶61; draft/09-claims.md claim 1 and claim 7; figures/fig-01.md, figures/fig-02.m) - The inventor says only that air "passes through perforations in the product tray" and never says where those perforations are. The candidate adds a specific location and distribution, carries it into claim 1 as a positive structural limitation of the tray and into claim 7 as a further limitation, and builds figure geometry on it. Location of an opening is a structure, and the candidate's own detailed description cannot supply support it introduced itself. The added location is also what produces the flow-path contradiction reported separately.
  - Suggested fix: Recite the perforations only as the inventor did. In ¶7 replace with "The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through the removable product tray 20." and delete "so that the interior of the removable product tray 20 communicates with the lower return passage 28."; in claim 1 replace "a bottom with perforations through the bottom" with "perforations through the removable product tray"; delete "and the perforations are distributed across the bottom of the removable product tray" from claim 7; in ¶61 delete the first sentence about the number and distribution of perforations; in fig-02.md change to "Perforation 26: small gaps through the wall of the tray 20 opening into the adjacent side supply passage 30" and in fig-01.md replace "a field of small round through holes distributed across the panel" with a corresponding wall depiction.
- **[critical] The circulation path is recited in two mutually exclusive directions in the same paragraph** (draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶23 (also ¶7, ¶61); draft/09-claims.md claim 1 wherein-clause and claim 16 final step) - With the perforations placed only through the tray bottom, air arriving in a side supply passage cannot reach those perforations before reaching the lower return passage: the return passage lies between them. The first sentence of ¶23 orders the path "side supply passages → perforations → lower return passage", while the very next sentence orders it "lower return passage → up through the bottom → payload" by stating that cooled air is delivered from below. ¶7 states the bottom perforations connect the tray interior to the return passage, which is the second order, and ¶61 states delivery runs "from the side supply passages 30 into the interior" through those same bottom holes, which is the first. Claims 1 and 16 both freeze the first order into the claim language. As written, no single geometry satisfies every statement.
  - Suggested fix: Apply the same correction as for the bottom-perforation limitation: with the perforations no longer confined to the tray bottom, the disclosed order (side supply passages → perforations → lower return passage) is self-consistent throughout.
