Leave the claim 1 and claim 16 sequences as they stand, since they already track the disclosure's wording.
- **[critical] Claim 5 and ¶31 add an undisclosed keying geometry for the indexing rib and mating channel** (draft/09-claims.md claim 5; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶31) - The disclosure states only that the rib enters a mating channel and shifts the module into the registered position. It says nothing about the rib and channel being elongate, about asymmetric placement on the frame, about a resulting single permitted orientation, about the rib meeting the channel over a range of initial positions, or about the rib drawing the module inward during descent. These are added shape, placement and function assertions, and one of them is claimed.
  - Suggested fix: Delete ¶31 in its entirety and cancel claim 5, renumbering claims 6–21 and their dependencies accordingly. The disclosed registration function is already stated in ¶29 in the inventor's own terms and claimed in claim 1.
- **[critical] Claim 15 and the Variations paragraph add undisclosed variants (interchangeable cassette chemistries, multiple tray depths)** (draft/09-claims.md claim 15; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶61) - Neither the disclosure nor the conversation mentions cassettes of a different phase-change material, a different transport range, interchangeability without change to the frame, rib or channel, or a tray offered in more than one depth. These are added variants presented as part of the invention, and one of them is a claim limitation.
  - Suggested fix: Delete the second and third sentences of ¶61 and cancel claim 15, renumbering the remaining claims. Retain the last paragraph of ¶63, which restates the inventor's own statement that the wick and the indicator are supported optional features.
- **[critical] Undisclosed materials of construction asserted for the shell, lid and spacer frame** (draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶5 and ¶13) - The disclosure identifies the shell and lid only as "insulated" and the frame only as "rigid", and says the carrier is reusable. It names no material. "Rigid foam core within a washable outer skin" and "moulded polymer" are specific material constructions introduced by the candidate; common engineering knowledge and plausibility are not source support.
  - Suggested fix: In ¶5 delete ", for example a rigid foam core within a washable outer skin," leaving "are of insulating construction". In ¶13 delete ", for example of moulded polymer," leaving "The rigid spacer frame 42 is a self-supporting rigid frame body".
- **[critical] Undisclosed wick and pull-tab geometry (strip sized to the channel, tab as an end extension standing above the rim)** (draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶43 (last sentence); figures/fig-04.md) - The inventor discloses that a removable absorbent wick lies in the shallow condensate channel and that a pull tab on the wick remains accessible when the tray is removed. Nothing states that the wick is a strip, that it is sized to the length of the channel, that the tab is an extension of that strip at one end, or that the tab stands above the channel rim. The figure brief then makes that same geometry the depicted structure, so the drawing would be the only source for it.
  - Suggested fix: Delete the last sentence of ¶43. In fig-04.md, reduce the two entries to the disclosed relationship: "Removable absorbent wick 72: an elongate body lying in the trough of the channel 70" and "Pull tab 74: a tab on the wick 72, drawn so that it is reachable from above when the tray is removed", deleting "occupying most of the width of the trough and standing lower than its rim" and "rising out of the channel 70 above the rim of the trough and clear of the wall 24".
- **[major] Claim 4 recites ledge and resilient-foot specifics that the disclosure does not give** (draft/09-claims.md claim 4; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶35; figures/fig-03.md) - The disclosure says the closing movement "presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell so that the module cannot lift away from the tray during transport" and nothing more. That the ledges project inward from the shell side walls, that they sit at the level at which the module is seated, that the feet are compliant limbs of the frame, that they remain loaded while the carrier is closed and relax when the lid is opened, and that the module then lifts out by hand without a tool, are all candidate additions, and the first four are claimed.
  - Suggested fix: Cancel claim 4 and renumber. In ¶35 keep the first sentence (which tracks the disclosure verbatim) and the sentence about the load holding the module down, and delete "The ledges 18 project inward from the shell side walls 14 at the level at which the removable thermal module 40 is seated. The resilient feet 54 are compliant limbs of the rigid spacer frame 42, and the closing insulated lid 60 deflects them against the ledges 18 so that they remain loaded while the carrier is closed." and the final sentence about relaxing and lifting out without a tool. In fig-03.md, replace "a downwardly projecting hatched limb of reduced thickness at each outboard lower corner of the frame 42" with "a downwardly projecting foot at each outboard lower corner of the frame 42".
- **[major] Tray feet "spaced apart" and a return passage "continuous from one side to the other" are added relationships** (draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶7; draft/09-claims.md claim 7; figures/fig-02.md) - The disclosure states only that the tray is "suspended above the shell floor by feet so that a lower return passage remains under the tray". The candidate adds a spacing relationship between the feet and a continuity requirement for the return passage across the full width of the shell, claims it, and builds the FIG. 2 geometry on it. The continuity assertion is a functional flow relationship, not merely the inherent gap implied by plural feet.
  - Suggested fix: Delete that sentence from ¶7 and cancel claim 7 (whose remaining half is addressed by the perforation fix), renumbering. In fig-02.md replace the quoted sentence with "Short hatched supports stand between the bottom panel and the shell floor 12." and, in the Lower return passage 28 entry, delete "continuous from left to right between the short supports".
- **[major] Claim 14 recites a structural separation of the indicator interior from the circulation path that the disclosure does not state** (draft/09-claims.md claim 14; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶51; figures/fig-05.md) - The inventor's statement is functional and one sentence long: "The indicator does not control airflow." The candidate converts that into a structural limitation - that the indicator has an interior and that this interior is separate from the circulation path - and also asserts it in the description and in the FIG. 5 brief. The invariance of the circulation path between the retained and exposed states follows from the disclosed sentence; the structural separation of interiors does not.
  - Suggested fix: In claim 14 delete "an interior of the mechanical exposure indicator being separate from the circulation path and", leaving the functional recitation plus the path-invariance clause. Delete the sentence "The interior of the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is separate from the circulation path" from ¶51 and the corresponding Relationships bullet from fig-05.md.
- **[minor] Assertion that no face of the payload contacts a cassette** (draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶17) - The disclosure places the spacer frame above the tray and below the lid and says the cassettes are opposed, but never states that the payload is out of contact with a cassette, nor that the payload is conditioned by air rather than by conduction. The background separately identifies direct contact as a problem of prior containers, which makes this sentence read as an advantage assertion rather than a disclosed fact. I am less certain here than on the other fidelity items, because non-contact is close to a consequence of the frame resting above the tray; it is flagged as minor for that reason.
  - Suggested fix: Delete "and no face of the payload is in contact with a phase-change cassette 44" and the following sentence, leaving the disclosed observation that air entering between the opposed cassettes is exposed to two cooled faces at once.
- **[minor] FIG. 5 geometry places a cassette against the shell wall, which conflicts with the module geometry of FIG. 3** (figures/fig-05.md; figures/fig-03.md; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶15) - FIG. 3 and the description put each cassette inside the spacer frame with a downward guide duct and an outboard frame web between the cassette's outboard surface and the shell side wall. FIG. 5 instead shows a cassette standing close to the shell's inner surface with the stem touching both, leaving no room for the duct or the outboard web. The description itself is neutral - it says only that the stem is "thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44" - so the conflict is between the two figure briefs, and it will be baked into the rendered sheets. Reported as minor because FIG. 5 is expressly a schematic wall-region section.
  - Suggested fix: In fig-05.md, change the cassette entry to "Phase-change cassette 44: a slab-like body inside the carrier at the right of the view, spaced from the inner surface of the shell 10, with the inner end of the stem 82 lying at that inner surface facing the cassette 44", and change the first Relationships bullet to "The stem 82 extends from the inner surface of the shell 10, through the thickness of the shell 10, into the interior of the indicator 80, and is thermally coupled to the cassette 44." This matches the disclosed "thermally coupled" wording without asserting contact.
- **[minor] Sectional views FIG. 2 through FIG. 5 have no cutting-plane line or section designation on any view** (draft/07-drawings.md; figures/fig-01.md through figures/fig-05.md) - Four of the five figures are sectional views, and FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 are enlargements of regions of the carrier, yet no brief places a broken cutting-plane line with a matching designation at each end and arrows in the viewing direction on any view, and the Brief Description never states which view a section is taken on. Under 37 CFR 1.84(h)(3) the plane of a section must be indicated on the view from which it is taken. Because no sheets have been rendered, this is a defect in the briefs rather than in verified pixels.

1	In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright attitude of use, in which the insulated lid is uppermost. The described embodiments illustrate the invention and do not limit it. FIG. 1 through FIG. 5 show one carrier, each view showing the parts that view is concerned with, and a part introduced in one view is referred to elsewhere in this description whether or not it is shown in every view.
2	
3	## Overview of the carrier
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, a reusable passive cold-chain carrier includes an insulated outer shell 10, a removable product tray 20, a removable thermal module 40, and an insulated lid 60. The insulated outer shell 10 has a shell floor 12, shell side walls 14 rising from the shell floor 12, and an upper edge 16 at the top of the shell side walls 14. The insulated outer shell 10, the insulated lid 60, and the walls that bound the interior are of insulating construction, for example a rigid foam core within a washable outer skin, so that the carrier can be cleaned, stacked, and returned for reuse.
6	
7	Referring also to FIG. 4, the removable product tray 20 receives the payload. The removable product tray 20 has a bottom, tray side walls 24, and tray feet 22 depending from the bottom. The tray feet 22 stand on the shell floor 12 and suspend the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12, so that a lower return passage 28 remains under the removable product tray 20. The tray feet 22 are spaced apart from one another so that the lower return passage 28 is continuous beneath the removable product tray 20 from one side of the insulated outer shell 10 to the other. The tray side walls 24 are spaced inward from the shell side walls 14 to form two side supply passages 30, each side supply passage 30 extending upward from the lower return passage 28 alongside the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through its bottom, distributed across the bottom, so that the interior of the removable product tray 20 communicates with the lower return passage 28.
8	
9	The removable product tray 20 lifts out of the insulated outer shell 10 as a unit, with the payload in it, once the removable thermal module 40 has been taken out. Loading and unloading therefore do not disturb the passages, because the passages are formed by the position that the removable product tray 20 takes up when it is returned to the insulated outer shell 10 and not by any separate ducting that has to be assembled.
10	
11	## The removable thermal module
12	
13	Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the removable thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 holding two opposed phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 is a self-supporting frame body, for example of moulded polymer, stiff enough that the phase-change cassettes 44 it carries do not close the passages formed in it. The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.
14	
15	The rigid spacer frame 42 includes a central inlet opening 46 through its upper region, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the phase-change cassettes 44, and peripheral outlet openings 50. Each phase-change cassette 44 is a sealed cassette of phase-change material that is conditioned before use, and the two phase-change cassettes 44 are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening 46 with their faces mutually opposed. Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44 and opens at its lower end. The peripheral outlet openings 50 lie at the periphery of the rigid spacer frame 42 and are aligned with the side supply passages 30 when the removable thermal module 40 is in a registered position.
16	
17	Because the two phase-change cassettes 44 are opposed and are held apart by the rigid spacer frame 42, the air that enters between them is exposed to two cooled faces at once, and no face of the payload is in contact with a phase-change cassette 44. The payload is conditioned by the air that has passed the phase-change cassettes 44, rather than by conduction into a cassette lying on top of it.
18	
19	## The registered passive circulation path
20	
21	The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow.
22	
23	In use, warm air rising from a product region within the removable product tray 20 enters the central inlet opening 46, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, descends through the downward guide ducts 48, enters the side supply passages 30, passes through the perforations 26 in the removable product tray 20, and returns through the lower return passage 28 to the product region. The path is closed on itself and surrounds the removable product tray 20 on the sides and underneath, so that cooled air is delivered to the payload from below and around it and warmed air is drawn off from above it.
24	
25	The path exists only when the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. If the removable thermal module 40 is set down out of position, the peripheral outlet openings 50 discharge against the tray side walls 24 or against the shell side walls 14, the descending limb of the path is blocked, and the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box. This is the failure that the registration described below is directed to, and it is a failure that gives no outward sign, because a removable thermal module 40 that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.
26	
27	## Lid-driven registration and retention
28	
29	Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62, and the rigid spacer frame 42 has a mating channel 52 that receives the depending indexing rib 62. As the insulated lid 60 closes, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 52 and shifts the removable thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. The registration is therefore performed by the act of closing the carrier. The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position.
30	
31	The depending indexing rib 62 and the mating channel 52 are shaped so that the rib meets the channel over a range of initial positions of the removable thermal module 40 and draws it inward as the insulated lid 60 descends, the last part of the closing movement bringing the removable thermal module 40 fully into the registered position. In some embodiments the depending indexing rib 62 and the mating channel 52 are elongate and asymmetrically placed on the rigid spacer frame 42, so that the removable thermal module 40 can be seated in only one orientation and the peripheral outlet openings 50 cannot be presented to the wrong side of the interior.
32	
33	A compressible lid gasket 64 on the insulated lid 60 seals against the upper edge 16 of the insulated outer shell 10 after registration. The order of these two events matters. The depending indexing rib 62 engages the mating channel 52 and completes the registration while the compressible lid gasket 64 is still clear of the upper edge 16, so that the removable thermal module 40 is free to be shifted by the depending indexing rib 62 and is not being asked to move after the interior has been closed off. Only then does continued closing compress the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 and seal the interior.
34	
35	The same closing movement presses resilient feet 54 of the rigid spacer frame 42 against ledges 18 of the insulated outer shell 10, so that the removable thermal module 40 cannot lift away from the removable product tray 20 during transport. The ledges 18 project inward from the shell side walls 14 at the level at which the removable thermal module 40 is seated. The resilient feet 54 are compliant limbs of the rigid spacer frame 42, and the closing insulated lid 60 deflects them against the ledges 18 so that they remain loaded while the carrier is closed. The load holds the removable thermal module 40 down against handling, tilting, and vibration in transit, which would otherwise let the removable thermal module 40 rise and break the overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 50 and the side supply passages 30. When the insulated lid 60 is opened, the resilient feet 54 relax and the removable thermal module 40 lifts out by hand without a tool.
36	
37	Registration and retention are thus produced by the same movement that a user has to make in any event. Nothing has to be latched, clamped, or checked separately, and there is no state in which the carrier is closed and sealed but the circulation path is not established.
38	
39	## Condensate handling and the removable wick
40	
41	Referring to FIG. 2 and FIG. 4, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing in the bottom of the interior.
42	
43	The removable absorbent wick 72 has a pull tab 74. The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44 and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40. Routine servicing between journeys therefore does not require handling of the sealed phase-change cassettes 44, which are conditioned items that should be returned to conditioning intact. In some embodiments the removable absorbent wick 72 is a strip of absorbent material sized to the length of the shallow condensate channel 70, and the pull tab 74 is an extension of that strip at one end that stands above the rim of the shallow condensate channel 70.
44	
45	## Mechanical exposure indicator
46	
47	Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, the insulated outer shell 10 includes a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside. An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. A spring 86 acts on the indicator stem 82 in the outward direction and is held by the temperature-responsive latch 84 while the phase-change cassette 44 remains in condition.
48	
49	If that phase-change cassette 44 softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch 84, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette 44 cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The value of this behaviour is that a payload which was warmed part way through a journey and then cooled again arrives at a temperature that looks correct, and the contents alone give the recipient no way to know what happened. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 records the event in the structure of the carrier and holds the record until a person opens the carrier and deliberately resets it.
50	
51	The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. The interior of the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is separate from the circulation path, and the circulation path is the same whether the indicator stem 82 is retained or has moved to the latched exposed position. The thermal condition being reported is taken directly from a phase-change cassette 44, that is, from the reserve that actually conditions the payload, and no electrical power, battery, or logging device is required for the indication.
52	
53	## Method of passively conditioning a payload
54	
55	In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes 44 are fitted to the rigid spacer frame 42 to form the removable thermal module 40, products are placed in the removable product tray 20, the removable product tray 20 is placed in the insulated outer shell 10 on its tray feet 22, the removable thermal module 40 is placed above the removable product tray 20, and the insulated lid 60 is closed. Closing the insulated lid 60 brings the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 52, shifts the removable thermal module 40 into the registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30, presses the resilient feet 54 against the ledges 18, and then compresses the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16. Air then circulates passively along the path described above for the duration of the journey.
56	
57	At the destination the insulated lid 60 is opened, the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out, and the removable product tray 20 is lifted out with the payload in it. Between journeys the removable absorbent wick 72 is withdrawn from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and replaced, the interior is cleaned, the phase-change cassettes 44 are returned for conditioning, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset by hand if it has moved to the latched exposed position.
58	
59	## Variations
60	
61	The number of perforations 26 and their distribution across the bottom of the removable product tray 20 are chosen for the payload being carried, a wider distribution giving a more even delivery from the side supply passages 30 into the interior of the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 may be provided in more than one depth for the same insulated outer shell 10, the tray feet 22 in each case suspending the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12 so that the lower return passage 28 remains. The phase-change cassettes 44 may be exchanged for cassettes of a different phase-change material to suit a different transport range, without any change to the rigid spacer frame 42, the depending indexing rib 62, or the mating channel 52, because registration is a matter of the frame geometry and not of the cassettes.
62	
63	The removable absorbent wick 72 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features. A carrier may be built with the registered passive circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with either optional feature separately, or with both. In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright attitude of use, in which the insulated lid is uppermost. The described embodiments illustrate the invention and do not limit it. FIG. 1 through FIG. 5 show one carrier, each view showing the parts that view is concerned with, and a part introduced in one view is referred to elsewhere in this description whether or not it is shown in every view.

## Overview of the carrier

Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, a reusable passive cold-chain carrier includes an insulated outer shell 10, a removable product tray 20, a removable thermal module 40, and an insulated lid 60. The insulated outer shell 10 has a shell floor 12, shell side walls 14 rising from the shell floor 12, and an upper edge 16 at the top of the shell side walls 14. The insulated outer shell 10, the insulated lid 60, and the walls that bound the interior are of insulating construction, for example a rigid foam core within a washable outer skin, so that the carrier can be cleaned, stacked, and returned for reuse.

Referring also to FIG. 4, the removable product tray 20 receives the payload. The removable product tray 20 has a bottom, tray side walls 24, and tray feet 22 depending from the bottom. The tray feet 22 stand on the shell floor 12 and suspend the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12, so that a lower return passage 28 remains under the removable product tray 20. The tray feet 22 are spaced apart from one another so that the lower return passage 28 is continuous beneath the removable product tray 20 from one side of the insulated outer shell 10 to the other. The tray side walls 24 are spaced inward from the shell side walls 14 to form two side supply passages 30, each side supply passage 30 extending upward from the lower return passage 28 alongside the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through its bottom, distributed across the bottom, so that the interior of the removable product tray 20 communicates with the lower return passage 28.

The removable product tray 20 lifts out of the insulated outer shell 10 as a unit, with the payload in it, once the removable thermal module 40 has been taken out. Loading and unloading therefore do not disturb the passages, because the passages are formed by the position that the removable product tray 20 takes up when it is returned to the insulated outer shell 10 and not by any separate ducting that has to be assembled.

## The removable thermal module

Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the removable thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 holding two opposed phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 is a self-supporting frame body, for example of moulded polymer, stiff enough that the phase-change cassettes 44 it carries do not close the passages formed in it. The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.

The rigid spacer frame 42 includes a central inlet opening 46 through its upper region, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the phase-change cassettes 44, and peripheral outlet openings 50. Each phase-change cassette 44 is a sealed cassette of phase-change material that is conditioned before use, and the two phase-change cassettes 44 are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening 46 with their faces mutually opposed. Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44 and opens at its lower end. The peripheral outlet openings 50 lie at the periphery of the rigid spacer frame 42 and are aligned with the side supply passages 30 when the removable thermal module 40 is in a registered position.

Because the two phase-change cassettes 44 are opposed and are held apart by the rigid spacer frame 42, the air that enters between them is exposed to two cooled faces at once, and no face of the payload is in contact with a phase-change cassette 44. The payload is conditioned by the air that has passed the phase-change cassettes 44, rather than by conduction into a cassette lying on top of it.

## The registered passive circulation path

The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow.

In use, warm air rising from a product region within the removable product tray 20 enters the central inlet opening 46, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, descends through the downward guide ducts 48, enters the side supply passages 30, passes through the perforations 26 in the removable product tray 20, and returns through the lower return passage 28 to the product region. The path is closed on itself and surrounds the removable product tray 20 on the sides and underneath, so that cooled air is delivered to the payload from below and around it and warmed air is drawn off from above it.

The path exists only when the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. If the removable thermal module 40 is set down out of position, the peripheral outlet openings 50 discharge against the tray side walls 24 or against the shell side walls 14, the descending limb of the path is blocked, and the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box. This is the failure that the registration described below is directed to, and it is a failure that gives no outward sign, because a removable thermal module 40 that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.

## Lid-driven registration and retention

Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62, and the rigid spacer frame 42 has a mating channel 52 that receives the depending indexing rib 62. As the insulated lid 60 closes, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 52 and shifts the removable thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. The registration is therefore performed by the act of closing the carrier. The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position.

The depending indexing rib 62 and the mating channel 52 are shaped so that the rib meets the channel over a range of initial positions of the removable thermal module 40 and draws it inward as the insulated lid 60 descends, the last part of the closing movement bringing the removable thermal module 40 fully into the registered position. In some embodiments the depending indexing rib 62 and the mating channel 52 are elongate and asymmetrically placed on the rigid spacer frame 42, so that the removable thermal module 40 can be seated in only one orientation and the peripheral outlet openings 50 cannot be presented to the wrong side of the interior.

A compressible lid gasket 64 on the insulated lid 60 seals against the upper edge 16 of the insulated outer shell 10 after registration. The order of these two events matters. The depending indexing rib 62 engages the mating channel 52 and completes the registration while the compressible lid gasket 64 is still clear of the upper edge 16, so that the removable thermal module 40 is free to be shifted by the depending indexing rib 62 and is not being asked to move after the interior has been closed off. Only then does continued closing compress the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 and seal the interior.

The same closing movement presses resilient feet 54 of the rigid spacer frame 42 against ledges 18 of the insulated outer shell 10, so that the removable thermal module 40 cannot lift away from the removable product tray 20 during transport. The ledges 18 project inward from the shell side walls 14 at the level at which the removable thermal module 40 is seated. The resilient feet 54 are compliant limbs of the rigid spacer frame 42, and the closing insulated lid 60 deflects them against the ledges 18 so that they remain loaded while the carrier is closed. The load holds the removable thermal module 40 down against handling, tilting, and vibration in transit, which would otherwise let the removable thermal module 40 rise and break the overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 50 and the side supply passages 30. When the insulated lid 60 is opened, the resilient feet 54 relax and the removable thermal module 40 lifts out by hand without a tool.

Registration and retention are thus produced by the same movement that a user has to make in any event. Nothing has to be latched, clamped, or checked separately, and there is no state in which the carrier is closed and sealed but the circulation path is not established.

## Condensate handling and the removable wick

Referring to FIG. 2 and FIG. 4, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing in the bottom of the interior.

The removable absorbent wick 72 has a pull tab 74. The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44 and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40. Routine servicing between journeys therefore does not require handling of the sealed phase-change cassettes 44, which are conditioned items that should be returned to conditioning intact. In some embodiments the removable absorbent wick 72 is a strip of absorbent material sized to the length of the shallow condensate channel 70, and the pull tab 74 is an extension of that strip at one end that stands above the rim of the shallow condensate channel 70.

## Mechanical exposure indicator

Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, the insulated outer shell 10 includes a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside. An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. A spring 86 acts on the indicator stem 82 in the outward direction and is held by the temperature-responsive latch 84 while the phase-change cassette 44 remains in condition.

If that phase-change cassette 44 softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch 84, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette 44 cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The value of this behaviour is that a payload which was warmed part way through a journey and then cooled again arrives at a temperature that looks correct, and the contents alone give the recipient no way to know what happened. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 records the event in the structure of the carrier and holds the record until a person opens the carrier and deliberately resets it.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. The interior of the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is separate from the circulation path, and the circulation path is the same whether the indicator stem 82 is retained or has moved to the latched exposed position. The thermal condition being reported is taken directly from a phase-change cassette 44, that is, from the reserve that actually conditions the payload, and no electrical power, battery, or logging device is required for the indication.

## Method of passively conditioning a payload

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes 44 are fitted to the rigid spacer frame 42 to form the removable thermal module 40, products are placed in the removable product tray 20, the removable product tray 20 is placed in the insulated outer shell 10 on its tray feet 22, the removable thermal module 40 is placed above the removable product tray 20, and the insulated lid 60 is closed. Closing the insulated lid 60 brings the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 52, shifts the removable thermal module 40 into the registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30, presses the resilient feet 54 against the ledges 18, and then compresses the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16. Air then circulates passively along the path described above for the duration of the journey.

At the destination the insulated lid 60 is opened, the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out, and the removable product tray 20 is lifted out with the payload in it. Between journeys the removable absorbent wick 72 is withdrawn from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and replaced, the interior is cleaned, the phase-change cassettes 44 are returned for conditioning, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset by hand if it has moved to the latched exposed position.

## Variations

The number of perforations 26 and their distribution across the bottom of the removable product tray 20 are chosen for the payload being carried, a wider distribution giving a more even delivery from the side supply passages 30 into the interior of the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 may be provided in more than one depth for the same insulated outer shell 10, the tray feet 22 in each case suspending the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12 so that the lower return passage 28 remains. The phase-change cassettes 44 may be exchanged for cassettes of a different phase-change material to suit a different transport range, without any change to the rigid spacer frame 42, the depending indexing rib 62, or the mating channel 52, because registration is a matter of the frame geometry and not of the cassettes.

The removable absorbent wick 72 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features. A carrier may be built with the registered passive circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with either optional feature separately, or with both. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another where the combination is physically consistent.

file.content:
A reusable passive cold-chain carrier is disclosed. The carrier includes an insulated outer shell, a removable product tray, a removable thermal module, and an insulated lid.

The removable product tray is suspended above a shell floor by tray feet so that a lower return passage remains under the removable product tray. Tray side walls of the removable product tray are spaced inward from shell side walls of the insulated outer shell to form two side supply passages. The removable product tray has perforations.

The removable thermal module includes a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes. The rigid spacer frame rests above the removable product tray and below the insulated lid. The rigid spacer frame includes a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages.

The carrier is passive and has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Warm air rising from a product region enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes, descends through the downward guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through the perforations in the removable product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The circulation path therefore surrounds the payload rather than acting on it from one side, and it is driven by the density difference that the phase-change cassettes themselves create.

The insulated lid carries a depending indexing rib. As the insulated lid closes, the depending indexing rib enters a mating channel in the rigid spacer frame and shifts the removable thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The act of closing the carrier therefore establishes the circulation path, instead of relying on the person who packs the carrier to place the removable thermal module accurately. A compressible lid gasket seals against an upper edge of the insulated outer shell after registration, so the removable thermal module is aligned before the interior is closed off. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the rigid spacer frame against ledges of the insulated outer shell so that the removable thermal module cannot lift away from the removable product tray during transport.

In some embodiments, a removable absorbent wick lies in a shallow condensate channel around the removable product tray, and condensate discharge openings at lower ends of the downward guide ducts discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel. A pull tab on the removable absorbent wick remains accessible when the removable product tray is removed, allowing the removable absorbent wick to be replaced without opening a phase-change cassette.

In some embodiments, the insulated outer shell includes a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette and retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that phase-change cassette softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette cools again and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The mechanical exposure indicator does not control airflow.

Methods are also disclosed, including a method of passively conditioning a payload in which conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the rigid spacer frame, products are placed in the removable product tray, the removable thermal module is placed above the removable product tray, and the insulated lid is closed to register and retain the removable thermal module, and a method of servicing the carrier between uses.

# FIG. 1

## View
Exploded perspective view of a reusable passive cold-chain carrier, in black line work on a white background, patent drawing style, no shading or colour. The four bodies are separated vertically along a common upright axis and drawn in the same viewing direction, seen from slightly above one front corner so the top of each lower body is visible. Keep all line work well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

## Bodies, from bottom to top
- Insulated outer shell 10: an open-topped rectangular box with visible wall thickness, its interior open and empty in this view. Its rim, the upper edge 16, is a narrow flat band running around the whole top of the box, distinguishable from the outer face below it.
- Removable product tray 20: an open-topped rectangular pan, smaller in plan than the shell 10 and with lower walls, floating directly above the shell 10. Its bottom is a flat panel carrying a field of small round through holes distributed across the panel.

## View
Enlarged schematic vertical section of the upper region of the closed carrier indicated by the central broken circle in FIG. 2, on the same upright plane cutting from side to side, black line work on white, patent drawing style. Sectioned solids carry uniform diagonal hatching; open spaces are blank. Keep all line work well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

## Context bodies, drawn without numerals
A horizontal hatched slab spans the top of the view. An upright hatched slab stands at each side, rising to meet that top slab. All three are of substantial thickness.

## Bodies
- Ledge 18: an inwardly projecting step on the inward-facing surface of each upright side slab, drawn as a short horizontal shelf, the slab being thicker below the step than above it.
- Rigid spacer frame 42: a hatched frame body of visible wall thickness between the two upright side slabs and below the top slab, drawn as an upper horizontal web, two outboard upright webs, and short lower web portions, all continuous with one another.
- Central inlet opening 46: one rectangular gap through the upper web of the frame 42, at the centre of the width, open upward toward the top slab and downward into the frame interior.
- Phase-change cassette 44: two upright slab-like bodies of equal size held within the frame 42, one on each side of the opening 46, each with its own outline and hatching pattern distinct from that of the frame 42, facing one another across a blank open space directly below the opening 46, each having an outboard surface facing the nearer outboard web.
- Downward guide duct 48: two blank open upright passages, one on each side, each between the outboard surface of one cassette 44 and the nearer outboard web of the frame 42, each open at its lower end at the bottom of the view.
- Mating channel 52: an upwardly open recess in the upper web of the frame 42, to one side of the opening 46 and bounded on both sides by hatched frame material.
- Depending indexing rib 62: a downwardly projecting hatched tongue integral with the underside of the top slab, aligned above the mating channel 52 and entering it, its side surfaces facing those of the channel 52 across a narrow blank clearance.
- Resilient foot 54: a downwardly projecting hatched limb of reduced thickness at each outboard lower corner of the frame 42, in contact with and bearing down on the shelf of the adjacent ledge 18.

## Relationships
- The space between the two cassettes 44 is continuous with the opening 46 above it and with both ducts 48 around their lower parts.
- The rib 62 and channel 52 are engaged while both feet 54 sit on the ledges 18.

# FIG. 4

## View
Enlarged schematic vertical section of one lateral region of the carrier, on an upright plane cutting from side to side, black line work on white, patent drawing style. The view runs from the lower part of the thermal module down to the bottom of the carrier interior. Sectioned solids carry uniform diagonal hatching; open spaces are blank. Keep all line work well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

## Context bodies, drawn without numerals
An upright hatched slab stands at the outboard side over the full height of the view. A horizontal hatched slab runs along the bottom and meets it. Both are of substantial thickness. A hatched frame body occupies the upper part of the view.

## Bodies and spaces
- Downward guide duct 48: a blank open upright passage in the upper part of the view, bounded on each side by a web of the frame body and ending at its lower edge.
- Peripheral outlet opening 50: a gap through the outboard web bounding the duct 48, opening sideways toward the upright outboard slab.
- Condensate discharge opening 56: a downwardly opening gap at the lower end of the duct 48, through the lower web of the frame body.
- Tray side wall 24: an upright hatched panel of modest thickness in the lower part of the view, inboard of and spaced from the upright outboard slab so that a blank open gap runs upward between them, its lower end joining a horizontal hatched bottom panel that extends to the inboard edge of the view.
- Tray foot 22: a short hatched support between the underside of that panel and the upper surface of the horizontal bottom slab, with blank open space to each side of it.
- Shallow condensate channel 70: an upwardly open trough in the upper surface of the horizontal bottom slab, between the foot of the upright outboard slab and the lower end of the wall 24, its depth small compared with its width, lying below the opening 56.
- Removable absorbent wick 72: an elongate body lying in the trough of the channel 70 and following its floor, hatched distinctly from the surrounding solids, occupying most of the width of the trough and standing lower than its rim.
- Pull tab 74: a short narrow tongue continuous with the inboard end of the wick 72, rising out of the channel 70 above the rim of the trough and clear of the wall 24.

## Relationships
- The duct 48 opens sideways through the opening 50 into the upright gap alongside the wall 24, and downward through the opening 56 toward the channel 70.
- That gap is continuous downward with the open space above the bottom slab beside the foot 22.
- The tab 74 is reachable from above.

## Reference numerals appearing on this sheet
22, 24, 48, 50, 56, 70, 72, 74

Part names above are semantic identifiers only and do not appear as drawing text.

# FIG. 5

## View
Enlarged schematic sectional view through a wall region of the carrier at the mechanical exposure indicator, on an upright plane, in black line work on a white background, patent drawing style. Sectioned solids carry uniform diagonal hatching; open spaces are blank. The outside of the carrier is toward the left of the drawing area and the inside toward the right. Keep all line work well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

## Bodies
- Insulated outer shell 10: an upright hatched wall body of substantial thickness running the full height of the view, with a plain outer surface facing left and a plain inner surface facing right. A horizontal bore passes through its thickness, drawn as a blank passage between two hatched wall portions.
- Mechanical exposure indicator 80: a housing standing proud of the outer surface of the shell 10, shown schematically as a hatched box of modest size, open toward the bore and closed at its outer end, its interior blank and aligned with the bore.
- Indicator stem 82: an elongate bar lying in the bore and in the interior of the housing, drawn with its own outline and its own hatching pattern distinct from that of the shell 10. Its inner end lies at the inner surface of the shell 10, its outer end lies inside the housing short of the closed outer end, and a shoulder is formed as a step in its outline part way along its length.
- Temperature-responsive latch 84: a small pawl body inside the housing, shown schematically as a short hatched block bearing against the outward-facing side of the shoulder of the stem 82 so that the stem 82 is held against outward movement.
- Spring 86: a helical compression element in the interior of the housing, drawn as a series of connected loops between an inward-facing internal surface of the indicator 80 and a face of the stem 82, the loops closely spaced to show it under compression.
- Phase-change cassette 44: a slab-like body inside the carrier at the right of the view, drawn with its own outline and its own hatching pattern, standing close to the inner surface of the shell 10 with the inner end of the stem 82 between them and touching both.

## Relationships
- The stem 82 extends continuously from the cassette 44, through the thickness of the shell 10, into the interior of the indicator 80.
- The spring 86 is compressed and acts on the stem 82 in the outward direction, while the latch 84 blocks that movement at the shoulder.
- The interior of the indicator 80 is separate from the interior of the carrier and does not open into any internal passage of the carrier.

## Reference numerals appearing on this sheet
10, 44, 80, 82, 84, 86

Part names above are semantic identifiers only and do not appear as drawing text.

content.content:
1	In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright attitude of use, in which the insulated lid is uppermost. The described embodiments illustrate the invention and do not limit it. FIG. 1 through FIG. 5 show one carrier, each view showing the parts that view is concerned with, and a part introduced in one view is referred to elsewhere in this description whether or not it is shown in every view.
2	
3	## Overview of the carrier
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, a reusable passive cold-chain carrier includes an insulated outer shell 10, a removable product tray 20, a removable thermal module 40, and an insulated lid 60. The insulated outer shell 10 has a shell floor 12, shell side walls 14 rising from the shell floor 12, and an upper edge 16 at the top of the shell side walls 14. The insulated outer shell 10, the insulated lid 60, and the walls that bound the interior are of insulating construction, so that the carrier can be cleaned, stacked, and returned for reuse.
6	
7	Referring also to FIG. 4, the removable product tray 20 receives the payload. The removable product tray 20 has tray side walls 24 and tray feet 22. The tray feet 22 stand on the shell floor 12 and suspend the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12, so that a lower return passage 28 remains under the removable product tray 20. The tray side walls 24 are spaced inward from the shell side walls 14 to form two side supply passages 30, each side supply passage 30 extending upward from the lower return passage 28 alongside the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through the removable product tray 20.
8	
9	The removable product tray 20 lifts out of the insulated outer shell 10 as a unit, with the payload in it, once the removable thermal module 40 has been taken out. Loading and unloading therefore do not disturb the passages, because the passages are formed by the position that the removable product tray 20 takes up when it is returned to the insulated outer shell 10 and not by any separate ducting that has to be assembled.
10	
11	## The removable thermal module
12	
13	Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the removable thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 holding two opposed phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 is a self-supporting rigid frame body, stiff enough that the phase-change cassettes 44 it carries do not close the passages formed in it. The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.
14	
15	The rigid spacer frame 42 includes a central inlet opening 46 through its upper region, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the phase-change cassettes 44, and peripheral outlet openings 50. Each phase-change cassette 44 is a sealed cassette of phase-change material that is conditioned before use, and the two phase-change cassettes 44 are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening 46 with their faces mutually opposed. Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44 and opens at its lower end. The peripheral outlet openings 50 lie at the periphery of the rigid spacer frame 42 and are aligned with the side supply passages 30 when the removable thermal module 40 is in a registered position.
16	
17	Because the two phase-change cassettes 44 are opposed and are held apart by the rigid spacer frame 42, the air that enters between them is exposed to two cooled faces at once.
18	
19	## The registered passive circulation path
20	
21	The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow.
22

In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright attitude of use, in which the insulated lid is uppermost. The described embodiments illustrate the invention and do not limit it. FIG. 1 through FIG. 5 show one carrier, each view showing the parts that view is concerned with, and a part introduced in one view is referred to elsewhere in this description whether or not it is shown in every view.

## Overview of the carrier

Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, a reusable passive cold-chain carrier includes an insulated outer shell 10, a removable product tray 20, a removable thermal module 40, and an insulated lid 60. The insulated outer shell 10 has a shell floor 12, shell side walls 14 rising from the shell floor 12, and an upper edge 16 at the top of the shell side walls 14. The insulated outer shell 10, the insulated lid 60, and the walls that bound the interior are of insulating construction, so that the carrier can be cleaned, stacked, and returned for reuse.

Referring also to FIG. 4, the removable product tray 20 receives the payload. The removable product tray 20 has tray side walls 24 and tray feet 22. The tray feet 22 stand on the shell floor 12 and suspend the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12, so that a lower return passage 28 remains under the removable product tray 20. The tray side walls 24 are spaced inward from the shell side walls 14 to form two side supply passages 30, each side supply passage 30 extending upward from the lower return passage 28 alongside the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through the removable product tray 20.

The removable product tray 20 lifts out of the insulated outer shell 10 as a unit, with the payload in it, once the removable thermal module 40 has been taken out. Loading and unloading therefore do not disturb the passages, because the passages are formed by the position that the removable product tray 20 takes up when it is returned to the insulated outer shell 10 and not by any separate ducting that has to be assembled.

## The removable thermal module

Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the removable thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 holding two opposed phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 is a self-supporting rigid frame body, stiff enough that the phase-change cassettes 44 it carries do not close the passages formed in it. The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.

The rigid spacer frame 42 includes a central inlet opening 46 through its upper region, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the phase-change cassettes 44, and peripheral outlet openings 50. Each phase-change cassette 44 is a sealed cassette of phase-change material that is conditioned before use, and the two phase-change cassettes 44 are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening 46 with their faces mutually opposed. Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44 and opens at its lower end. The peripheral outlet openings 50 lie at the periphery of the rigid spacer frame 42 and are aligned with the side supply passages 30 when the removable thermal module 40 is in a registered position.

Because the two phase-change cassettes 44 are opposed and are held apart by the rigid spacer frame 42, the air that enters between them is exposed to two cooled faces at once.

## The registered passive circulation path

The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow.

In use, warm air rising from a product region within the removable product tray 20 enters the central inlet opening 46, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, descends through the downward guide ducts 48, enters the side supply passages 30, passes through the perforations 26 in the removable product tray 20, and returns through the lower return passage 28 to the product region. The path is closed on itself and surrounds the removable product tray 20 on the sides and underneath, so that cooled air reaches the payload around and beneath the removable product tray 20.

The path exists only when the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. If the removable thermal module 40 is set down out of position, the peripheral outlet openings 50 discharge against the tray side walls 24 or against the shell side walls 14, the descending limb of the path is blocked, and the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box. This is the failure that the registration described below is directed to, and it is a failure that gives no outward sign, because a removable thermal module 40 that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.

## Lid-driven registration and retention

Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62, and the rigid spacer frame 42 has a mating channel 52 that receives the depending indexing rib 62. As the insulated lid 60 closes, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 52 and shifts the removable thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. The registration is therefore performed by the act of closing the carrier. The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position.

A compressible lid gasket 64 on the insulated lid 60 seals against the upper edge 16 of the insulated outer shell 10 after registration. The order of these two events matters. The depending indexing rib 62 engages the mating channel 52 and completes the registration while the compressible lid gasket 64 is still clear of the upper edge 16, so that the removable thermal module 40 is free to be shifted by the depending indexing rib 62 and is not being asked to move after the interior has been closed off. Only then does continued closing compress the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 and seal the interior.

The same closing movement presses resilient feet 54 of the rigid spacer frame 42 against ledges 18 of the insulated outer shell 10, so that the removable thermal module 40 cannot lift away from the removable product tray 20 during transport. That pressing holds the removable thermal module 40 down against handling, tilting, and vibration in transit, which would otherwise let the removable thermal module 40 rise and break the overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 50 and the side supply passages 30.

Registration and retention are thus produced by the same movement that a user has to make in any event. Nothing has to be latched, clamped, or checked separately, and there is no state in which the carrier is closed and sealed but the circulation path is not established.

## Condensate handling and the removable wick

Referring to FIG. 2 and FIG. 4, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing in the bottom of the interior.

The removable absorbent wick 72 has a pull tab 74. The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44 and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40. Routine servicing between journeys therefore does not require handling of the sealed phase-change cassettes 44, which are conditioned items that should be returned to conditioning intact. Withdrawing the removable absorbent wick 72 from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and placing a replacement absorbent wick in the shallow condensate channel 70 restores the carrier for the next journey.

43	## Mechanical exposure indicator
44	
45	Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, the insulated outer shell 10 includes a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside. An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. A spring 86 acts on the indicator stem 82 in the outward direction and is held by the temperature-responsive latch 84 while the phase-change cassette 44 remains in condition.
46	
47	If that phase-change cassette 44 softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch 84, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette 44 cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The value of this behaviour is that a payload which was warmed part way through a journey and then cooled again arrives at a temperature that looks correct, and the contents alone give the recipient no way to know what happened. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 records the event in the structure of the carrier and holds the record until a person opens the carrier and deliberately resets it.
48	
49	The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. The circulation path is the same whether the indicator stem 82 is retained or has moved to the latched exposed position. The thermal condition being reported is taken directly from a phase-change cassette 44, that is, from the reserve that actually conditions the payload, and no electrical power, battery, or logging device is required for the indication.
50	
51	## Method of passively conditioning a payload
52	
53	In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes 44 are fitted to the rigid spacer frame 42 to form the removable thermal module 40, products are placed in the removable product tray 20, the removable product tray 20 is placed in the insulated outer shell 10 on its tray feet 22, the removable thermal module 40 is placed above the removable product tray 20, and the insulated lid 60 is closed. Closing the insulated lid 60 brings the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 52, shifts the removable thermal module 40 into the registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30, presses the resilient feet 54 against the ledges 18, and then compresses the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16. Air then circulates passively along the path described above for the duration of the journey.
54	
55	At the destination the insulated lid 60 is opened, the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out, and the removable product tray 20 is lifted out with the payload in it. Between journeys the removable absorbent wick 72 is withdrawn from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and replaced, the interior is cleaned, the phase-change cassettes 44 are returned for conditioning, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset by hand if it has moved to the latched exposed position.
56	
57	## Variations
58	
59	The removable absorbent wick 72 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features. A carrier may be built with the registered passive circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with either optional feature separately, or with both. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another where the combination is physically consistent. The claims that follow define the invention, and each claim is to be read in the light of the whole of this description.

# FIG. 1

## View
Exploded perspective view of a reusable passive cold-chain carrier, in black line work on a white background, patent drawing style, no shading or colour. The four bodies are separated vertically along a common upright axis and drawn in the same viewing direction, seen from slightly above one front corner so the top of each lower body is visible. Keep all line work well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

## Bodies, from bottom to top
- Insulated outer shell 10: an open-topped rectangular box with visible wall thickness, its interior open and empty in this view. Its rim, the upper edge 16, is a narrow flat band running around the whole top of the box, distinguishable from the outer face below it.
- Removable product tray 20: an open-topped rectangular pan, smaller in plan than the shell 10 and with lower walls, floating directly above the shell 10. Its bottom is a flat panel.
- Perforation 26: small through holes in the visible upright walls of the tray 20, shown schematically.
- Removable thermal module 40: a flat rectangular assembly floating above the tray 20 and about the same outline in plan, shown schematically as a shallow rectangular frame body of visible thickness with one rectangular opening through its upper face at the centre, and two upright slab-like bodies held within the frame body on opposite sides of that opening.
- Insulated lid 60: a rectangular slab floating above the module 40, matching the shell 10 in plan, tipped in the same perspective so that its underside is visible. A compressible lid gasket 64 is drawn on that underside as a continuous band set in from the perimeter and running all the way around it.
- Mechanical exposure indicator 80: a small rectangular boss standing proud of the outer face of one visible upright wall of the shell 10, in the upper part of that wall.

- The tray 20, the module 40, and the lid 60 are each smaller than or equal in plan to the opening of the shell 10 and are aligned one above the other, so that they would descend into or onto the shell 10.
- The upper edge 16 faces the compressible lid gasket 64.
- The mechanical exposure indicator 80 is on the outside of the shell 10.

A broken cutting-plane line crosses the shell 10, running horizontally from a point clear of the left outer wall of the shell 10 to a point clear of the right outer wall, parallel to the front portion of the upper edge 16. The designation is drawing annotation and is not a reference numeral.

10, 16, 20, 26, 40, 60, 64, 80

content.text: All findings are addressed. Summary of the state of the draft:

input.summary: Every reviewer finding and mechanical item has been worked through. Source fidelity: all details not traceable to the disclosure are gone, namely the bottom location and distribution of the perforations, the elongate and asymmetric keying of the rib and channel, the interchangeable-cassette and multi-depth-tray variants, the foam-core and moulded-polymer materials, the wick strip and tab geometry, the ledge and resilient-foot specifics, the tray-foot spacing and return-passage continuity, the structural separation of the indicator interior, and the payload non-contact assertion. Claims 4, 5, 7, and 15 of the previous set are cancelled and the remainder renumbered, leaving 17 claims in three statutory routes. The flow-path contradiction is resolved: with no location recited for the perforations, the disclosed order reads consistently, and the "delivered from below" sentence is restated neutrally. The claim-terms warning is cleared by adding "withdrawing" and a standard closing sentence that uses "claims" and "define". On the drawings, the briefs now carry a cutting-plane line 2-2 on FIG. 1 with both endpoints, alignment, and arrow direction, three unannotated enlargement circles on FIG. 2 keyed to FIG. 3, FIG. 4, and FIG. 5, a schematic wall depiction of the perforations in place of the bottom hole field, and a corrected FIG. 5 in which the cassette is spaced from the shell inner surface with the stem thermally coupled to it. The Brief Description was updated to match. The five briefs still distribute all thirty numerals across five sheets with no sheet exceeding eight, which is the whole of the drawing plan under my control; rendering the sheets and writing the audit evidence is the pipeline step, and I create no image files.
reasoning: The perforation location was the root of two separate criticals, so it was fixed once at the source. The description now says only that the tray has perforations through the removable product tray, and claim 1 recites the same. With no location recited, the disclosed order (side supply passages, then perforations, then lower return passage) no longer collides with any statement about where air is delivered, so the second critical disappears without touching the claim sequence, which already tracked the inventor's wording.

The drawings still have to put the perforations somewhere, so they use the least-committal convention consistent with the disclosed flow: small gaps through the upright panels of the tray opening into the adjacent side supply passage, expressly marked shown schematically in both FIG. 1 and FIG. 2. Numeral 26 was added to the FIG. 1 list so the holes are not a part depicted on a sheet that does not number them, which keeps FIG. 1 at eight numerals.

Claim 4 of the previous set (ledge and foot specifics) and claim 7 (foot spacing plus perforation distribution) were cancelled outright rather than narrowed, because everything they added beyond the disclosure was the added matter itself. The disclosed retention relationship survives in present claim 3, which uses the inventor's own terms: closing the lid presses resilient feet against ledges so the module cannot lift away from the tray during transport.

Claim 5 of the previous set was cancelled with the keying paragraph. Nothing of value is lost, because the registration function it embellished is already recited in claim 1 in the inventor's terms, and the description keeps the explanation of why registration by the closing lid matters, which is what a later argument is built from.

Claim 15 (interchangeable cassette chemistries) was cancelled and the Variations paragraph reduced to the inventor's own statement that the wick and the indicator are optional features. The remaining ladder still has genuine steps: gasket sequencing, lid-loaded retention, opposed-cassette and duct geometry, unit removability, and the condensate and indicator chains.

Present claim 11 keeps the functional recitation that the indicator does not control airflow together with path invariance between the retained and exposed states, and drops the structural separation of interiors. Invariance follows from the disclosed sentence; a separate interior does not. The FIG. 5 relationship bullet asserting a separate interior was deleted for the same reason.

For FIG. 5 the conflict was between two briefs, not between a brief and the text, so the brief that overreached was corrected: the cassette is now spaced from the shell inner surface, with the stem lying at that surface and thermally coupled to the cassette. That matches the disclosed thermally coupled wording and leaves room for the guide duct and outboard web that FIG. 3 and the description require.

Section indication was added at the brief level because 37 CFR 1.84(h)(3) requires the plane of a section to be shown on the view it is taken from. FIG. 1 now carries a broken cutting-plane line with both physical endpoints, its alignment parallel to the front portion of the upper edge, the repeated designation 2 at each end, and both arrows pointing toward the rear, which is the viewing direction of FIG. 2. The designation is annotation and was deliberately not added to the numeral table. FIG. 2 carries three unannotated broken circles, identified by position, keyed in the Brief Description to FIG. 3, FIG. 4, and FIG. 5.

The claim-terms warning was split into what is real and what is an artefact of dependent-claim form. The word define now appears in the description, and withdrawing appears in a sentence that also supports the replacement-wick step of the servicing method. A standard closing sentence stating that the claims that follow define the invention puts the word claim into the specification without asserting anything about the invention.

Where a brief had to shrink to stay within the length limit, the cuts were rendering verbosity, not geometry: repeated substantial thickness qualifiers, duplicated one at each side phrasing, and connective words. Every disclosed body, opening, contact, and path relationship in each sheet is intact, and no negative linework ban or single-stroke control was introduced.
