input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged in substance, since prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the directory holds no reference files, so the draft carries no citations. The cancellations did not touch the feature that carries claim 1: the peripheral outlet openings must overlap the side supply passages for the circulation path to exist, and that overlap is produced by the depending indexing rib entering the mating channel as the insulated lid closes, in a carrier having no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Cancelling the keying, ledge-detail, foot-spacing, and cassette-interchange claims removed only added matter, so the ladder is now shorter but every rung is disclosure-backed and independently arguable: gasket sealing sequenced after registration, lid-loaded retention against transport lift, the opposed-cassette and guide-duct geometry, unit removability of module and loaded tray, the condensate channel and wick chain including replacement without opening a cassette, and the irreversible exposure indicator chain including path invariance. The packing method and the depot servicing method remain as separate statutory routes reaching different infringers. The description still states the technical problem the registration solves, namely that a module set down out of position silently defeats the path, which is the passage a later argument would rest on. Because no search was run, claim 1 should be re-tested against real art before filing.
input.answer:
All findings are addressed.

**Source fidelity.** Everything the reviewer traced to me rather than to the inventor is out of the draft. The perforations are now recited exactly as disclosed, as perforations through the removable product tray, with no location and no distribution. Gone with them: the rib and channel keying paragraph, the interchangeable-cassette and multi-depth-tray variants, the foam-core and moulded-polymer materials, the wick strip and tab geometry, the ledge and foot specifics, the tray-foot spacing and return-passage continuity, the structural separation of the indicator interior, and the payload non-contact assertion.

**Claims.** The previous claims 4, 5, 7, and 15 are cancelled and the set renumbered to 17: claims 1 to 11 apparatus, claim 12 with 13 to 15 the packing method, claim 16 with 17 the servicing method. Claim 1 now recites the perforations without location, and claim 11 keeps the functional "does not control airflow" recitation with path invariance while dropping the separate-interior limitation.

**Flow-path contradiction.** Resolved at its source. With no location recited, the disclosed order reads consistently everywhere, and the sentence that had asserted delivery from below now states neutrally that cooled air reaches the payload around and beneath the tray. The claim sequences were left as they stood, since they already tracked the disclosure.

**Claim-terms warning.** "define" and "withdrawing" now appear in the description, the latter in a sentence that also supports the replacement-wick step of the servicing method, and a standard closing sentence puts "claims" into the specification.

**Drawings.** FIG. 1 now specifies a broken cutting-plane line across the shell with both endpoints, its alignment, the repeated designation 2 at each end so it reads as line 2-2, and both arrows pointing toward the rear as the viewing direction of FIG. 2; the designation is annotation and is not in the numeral table. FIG. 2 carries three unannotated broken circles, identified by position and keyed in the Brief Description to FIG. 3, FIG. 4, and FIG. 5. The perforations are drawn as a schematic wall depiction in both FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, with numeral 26 added to the FIG. 1 list so no depicted part goes unnumbered on its sheet. In FIG. 5 the cassette is spaced from the shell inner surface with the stem thermally coupled to it, which removes the conflict with the module geometry of FIG. 3.

**Synchronization.** The numeral table is unchanged and all 30 numerals still appear in the description and across the five sheets, which carry 8, 8, 8, 8, and 6 numerals. Every brief is at or below 2800 characters, the abstract stays at 140 words, and no placeholder, note, or em dash appears anywhere.

**On the missing sheets.** The two mechanical failures both stem from there being no rendered image for any figure. The drawing plan itself is complete and every numeral has a home; what remains is the rendering step, which runs outside this turn, and I create no image files. The briefs are final and self-contained so that each sheet can be generated from the text as it stands.

Claims 4, 5, 7, and 15 of the previous set are cancelled and the remainder renumbered, leaving 17 claims in three statutory routes. The flow-path contradiction is resolved: with no location recited for the perforations, the disclosed order reads consistently, and the "delivered from below" sentence is restated neutrally. The claim-terms warning is cleared by adding "withdrawing" and a standard closing sentence that uses "claims" and "define". On the drawings, the briefs now carry a cutting-plane line 2-2 on FIG. 1 with both endpoints, alignment, and arrow direction, three unannotated enlargement circles on FIG. 2 keyed to FIG. 3, FIG. 4, and FIG. 5, a schematic wall depiction of the perforations in place of the bottom hole field, and a corrected FIG. 5 in which the cassette is spaced from the shell inner surface with the stem thermally coupled to it. reasoning: The perforation location was the root of two separate criticals, so it was fixed once at the source. The description now says only that the tray has perforations through the removable product tray, and claim 1 recites the same. With no location recited, the disclosed order (side supply passages, then perforations, then lower return passage) no longer collides with any statement about where air is delivered, so the second critical disappears without touching the claim sequence, which already tracked the inventor's wording.

The drawings still have to put the perforations somewhere, so they use the least-committal convention consistent with the disclosed flow: small gaps through the upright panels of the tray opening into the adjacent side supply passage, expressly marked shown schematically in both FIG. 1 and FIG. 2. Numeral 26 was added to the FIG. 1 list so the holes are not a part depicted on a sheet that does not number them, which keeps FIG. 1 at eight numerals.

Claim 4 of the previous set (ledge and foot specifics) and claim 7 (foot spacing plus perforation distribution) were cancelled outright rather than narrowed, because everything they added beyond the disclosure was the added matter itself. The disclosed retention relationship survives in present claim 3, which uses the inventor's own terms: closing the lid presses resilient feet against ledges so the module cannot lift away from the tray during transport.

Claim 5 of the previous set was cancelled with the keying paragraph. Nothing of value is lost, because the registration function it embellished is already recited in claim 1 in the inventor's terms, and the description keeps the explanation of why registration by the closing lid matters, which is what a later argument is built from.

Claim 15 (interchangeable cassette chemistries) was cancelled and the Variations paragraph reduced to the inventor's own statement that the wick and the indicator are optional features. The remaining ladder still has genuine steps: gasket sequencing, lid-loaded retention, opposed-cassette and duct geometry, unit removability, and the condensate and indicator chains.

Present claim 11 keeps the functional recitation that the indicator does not control airflow together with path invariance between the retained and exposed states, and drops the structural separation of interiors. Invariance follows from the disclosed sentence; a separate interior does not. The FIG. 5 relationship bullet asserting a separate interior was deleted for the same reason.

For FIG. 5 the conflict was between two briefs, not between a brief and the text, so the brief that overreached was corrected: the cassette is now spaced from the shell inner surface, with the stem lying at that surface and thermally coupled to the cassette. That matches the disclosed thermally coupled wording and leaves room for the guide duct and outboard web that FIG. 3 and the description require.

Section indication was added at the brief level because 37 CFR 1.84(h)(3) requires the plane of a section to be shown on the view it is taken from. FIG. 1 now carries a broken cutting-plane line with both physical endpoints, its alignment parallel to the front portion of the upper edge, the repeated designation 2 at each end, and both arrows pointing toward the rear, which is the viewing direction of FIG. 2. The designation is annotation and was deliberately not added to the numeral table. FIG. 2 carries three unannotated broken circles, identified by position, keyed in the Brief Description to FIG. 3, FIG. 4, and FIG. 5.

The claim-terms warning was split into what is real and what is an artefact of dependent-claim form. The word define now appears in the description, and withdrawing appears in a sentence that also supports the replacement-wick step of the servicing method. A standard closing sentence stating that the claims that follow define the invention puts the word claim into the specification without asserting anything about the invention.

Where a brief had to shrink to stay within the length limit, the cuts were rendering verbosity, not geometry: repeated substantial thickness qualifiers, duplicated one at each side phrasing, and connective words. Every disclosed body, opening, contact, and path relationship in each sheet is intact, and no negative linework ban or single-stroke control was introduced.

data.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged in substance, since prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the directory holds no reference files, so the draft carries no citations. The cancellations did not touch the feature that carries claim 1: the peripheral outlet openings must overlap the side supply passages for the circulation path to exist, and that overlap is produced by the depending indexing rib entering the mating channel as the insulated lid closes, in a carrier having no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Cancelling the keying, ledge-detail, foot-spacing, and cassette-interchange claims removed only added matter, so the ladder is now shorter but every rung is disclosure-backed and independently arguable: gasket sealing sequenced after registration, lid-loaded retention against transport lift, the opposed-cassette and guide-duct geometry, unit removability of module and loaded tray, the condensate channel and wick chain including replacement without opening a cassette, and the irreversible exposure indicator chain including path invariance. The packing method and the depot servicing method remain as separate statutory routes reaching different infringers. The description still states the technical problem the registration solves, namely that a module set down out of position silently defeats the path, which is the passage a later argument would rest on. **Flow-path contradiction.** Resolved at its source. With no location recited, the disclosed order reads consistently everywhere, and the sentence that had asserted delivery from below now states neutrally that cooled air reaches the payload around and beneath the tray. The perforations are drawn as a schematic wall depiction in both FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, with numeral 26 added to the FIG. 1 list so no depicted part goes unnumbered on its sheet. In FIG. 5 the cassette is spaced from the shell inner surface with the stem thermally coupled to it, which removes the conflict with the module geometry of FIG. 3.

**Synchronization.** The numeral table is unchanged and all 30 numerals still appear in the description and across the five sheets, which carry 8, 8, 8, 8, and 6 numerals. Every brief is at or below 2800 characters, the abstract stays at 140 words, and no placeholder, note, or em dash appears anywhere.

**On the missing sheets.** The two mechanical failures both stem from there being no rendered image for any figure. The drawing plan itself is complete and every numeral has a home; what remains is the rendering step, which runs outside this turn, and I create no image files. The briefs are final and self-contained so that each sheet can be generated from the text as it stands.

# FIG. 1

## View
Exploded perspective view of a reusable passive cold-chain carrier, black line work on white, patent drawing style. The four bodies are separated vertically along a common upright axis, seen from slightly above one front corner so the top of each lower body is visible. Keep all line work well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

## Bodies, from bottom to top
- Insulated outer shell 10: an open-topped rectangular box with visible wall thickness, its interior open and empty in this view. Its rim, the upper edge 16, is a narrow flat band running around the whole top of the box, distinguishable from the outer face below it.
- Removable product tray 20: an open-topped rectangular pan, smaller in plan than the shell 10 and with lower walls, floating directly above the shell 10. Its bottom is a flat panel.
- Perforation 26: small through holes in the visible upright walls of the tray 20, shown schematically.
- Removable thermal module 40: a flat rectangular assembly floating above the tray 20 and about the same outline in plan, shown schematically as a shallow rectangular frame body of visible thickness with one rectangular opening through its upper face at the centre, and two upright slab-like bodies held within the frame body on opposite sides of that opening.
- Insulated lid 60: a rectangular slab floating above the module 40, matching the shell 10 in plan, tipped in the same perspective so that its underside is visible. A compressible lid gasket 64 is drawn on that underside as a continuous band set in from the perimeter and running all the way around it.
- Mechanical exposure indicator 80: a small rectangular boss standing proud of the outer face of one visible upright wall of the shell 10, in the upper part of that wall.

## Relationships
- The tray 20, the module 40, and the lid 60 are each smaller than or equal in plan to the opening of the shell 10 and are aligned one above the other, so that they would descend into or onto the shell 10.
- The upper edge 16 faces the compressible lid gasket 64.

## Cutting-plane line
A broken cutting-plane line crosses the shell 10 horizontally, from a point clear of its left outer wall to a point clear of its right outer wall, parallel to the front portion of the upper edge 16. The repeated designation 2 appears at both ends, so the line is line 2-2, and an arrow at each end points toward the rear of the shell 10, the direction in which the section of FIG. 2 is viewed. The designation is drawing annotation, not a reference numeral.

## Reference numerals appearing on this sheet
10, 16, 20, 26, 40, 60, 64, 80

Part names above are semantic identifiers only and do not appear as drawing text.

invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,

Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a

Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than

# FIG. 1

## View
Exploded perspective view of a reusable passive cold-chain carrier, black line work on white, patent drawing style. The four bodies are separated vertically along a common upright axis, seen from slightly above one front corner so the top of each lower body is visible. Keep all line work well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges and filing margins.

## Bodies, from bottom to top
- Insulated outer shell 10: an open-topped rectangular box with visible wall thickness, its interior open and empty in this view. Its rim, the upper edge 16, is a narrow flat band running around the whole top of the box.
- Removable product tray 20: an open-topped rectangular pan, smaller in plan than the shell 10 and with lower walls, floating directly above the shell 10.
- Perforation 26: small through holes in the visible upright walls of the tray 20 and in its bottom panel, shown schematically.
- Removable thermal module 40: a flat rectangular assembly floating above the tray 20 and about the same outline in plan, shown schematically as a shallow rectangular frame body of visible thickness with one rectangular opening through its upper face at the centre, and two upright slab-like bodies held within the frame body on opposite sides of that opening.
- Insulated lid 60: a rectangular slab floating above the module 40, matching the shell 10 in plan, tipped in the same perspective so that its underside is visible. A compressible lid gasket 64 is drawn on that underside as a continuous band set in from the perimeter and running all the way around it.
- Depending indexing rib 62: a short straight rib projecting downward from the underside of the lid 60, shown schematically, inboard of the gasket 64 and above the module 40.

## Relationships
- The tray 20, the module 40, and the lid 60 are each smaller than or equal in plan to the opening of the shell 10 and are aligned one above the other, so that they would descend into or onto the shell 10.
- The upper edge 16 faces the compressible lid gasket 64.

## Cutting-plane line
A broken cutting-plane line crosses each of the lid 60, the module 40, the tray 20, and the shell 10 horizontally at the same position across the common upright axis, each segment running from a point clear of the left outer wall of that body to a point clear of its right outer wall, parallel to the front portion of the upper edge 16. Together the segments are line 2-2, the same section designation being repeated at each end of the line, and an arrow at each end points toward the rear, the direction in which the section of FIG. 2 is viewed. 1	In the following description, the terms upper, lower, above, below, inward, and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright attitude of use, in which the insulated lid is uppermost. The described embodiments illustrate the invention and do not limit it. FIG. 1 through FIG. 6 show one carrier, each view showing the parts that view is concerned with, and a part introduced in one view is referred to elsewhere in this description whether or not it is shown in every view.
2	
3	## Overview of the carrier
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, a reusable passive cold-chain carrier includes an insulated outer shell 10, a removable product tray 20, a removable thermal module 40, and an insulated lid 60. The insulated outer shell 10 has a shell floor 12, shell side walls 14 rising from the shell floor 12, and an upper edge 16 at the top of the shell side walls 14. The insulated outer shell 10, the insulated lid 60, and the walls that bound the interior are of insulating construction, so that the carrier can be returned for reuse.
6	
7	Referring also to FIG. 5, the removable product tray 20 receives the payload. The removable product tray 20 has tray side walls 24 and tray feet 22. The tray feet 22 stand on the shell floor 12 and suspend the removable product tray 20 above the shell floor 12, so that a lower return passage 28 remains under the removable product tray 20. The tray side walls 24 are spaced inward from the shell side walls 14 to form two side supply passages 30, each side supply passage 30 extending upward from the lower return passage 28 alongside the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 has perforations 26 through the removable product tray 20.
8	
9	The removable product tray 20 lifts out of the insulated outer shell 10 as a unit, with the payload in it, once the removable thermal module 40 has been taken out. Loading and unloading therefore do not disturb the passages, because the passages are formed by the position that the removable product tray 20 takes up when it is returned to the insulated outer shell 10 and not by any separate ducting that has to be assembled.
10	
11	## The removable thermal module
12	
13	Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the removable thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 holding two opposed phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 is a rigid frame body that holds the two phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.
14	
15	The rigid spacer frame 42 includes a central inlet opening 46 through its upper region, two downward guide ducts 48 beside the phase-change cassettes 44, and peripheral outlet openings 50. Each phase-change cassette 44 is a sealed cassette of phase-change material that is conditioned before use, and the two phase-change cassettes 44 are held on opposite sides of the central inlet opening 46 with their faces mutually opposed. Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44 and opens at its lower end. The peripheral outlet openings 50 lie at the periphery of the rigid spacer frame 42 and are aligned with the side supply passages 30 when the removable thermal module 40 is in a registered position.
16	
17	Because the two phase-change cassettes 44 are opposed and are held apart by the rigid spacer frame 42, the air that enters between them is exposed to two cooled faces at once.
18	
19	## The registered passive circulation path
20	
21	The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow.
22	
23	In use, warm air rising from a product region within the removable product tray 20 enters the central inlet opening 46, divides along faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, descends through the downward guide ducts 48, enters the side supply passages 30, passes through the perforations 26 in the removable product tray 20, and returns through the lower return passage 28 to the product region. The path is closed on itself and surrounds the removable product tray 20 on the sides and underneath, so that cooled air reaches the payload around and beneath the removable product tray 20.
24	
25	The path exists only when the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. If the removable thermal module 40 is set down out of position, the peripheral outlet openings 50 discharge against the tray side walls 24 or against the shell side walls 14, the descending limb of the path is blocked, and the carrier behaves as a plain insulated box. This is the failure that the registration described below is directed to, and it is a failure that gives no outward sign, because a removable thermal module 40 that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.
26	
27	## Lid-driven registration and retention
28	
29	Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62, and the rigid spacer frame 42 has a mating channel 52 that receives the depending indexing rib 62. As the insulated lid 60 closes, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 52 and shifts the removable thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30. The registration is therefore performed by the act of closing the carrier. The person who packs the carrier is not required to align the removable thermal module 40, and cannot leave it misaligned, because the insulated lid 60 does not come down onto the upper edge 16 without carrying the removable thermal module 40 into position.
30	
31	A compressible lid gasket 64 on the insulated lid 60 seals against the upper edge 16 of the insulated outer shell 10 after registration. The order of these two events matters. The depending indexing rib 62 engages the mating channel 52 and completes the registration while the compressible lid gasket 64 is still clear of the upper edge 16, so that the removable thermal module 40 is free to be shifted by the depending indexing rib 62 and is not being asked to move after the interior has been closed off. Only then does continued closing compress the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16 and seal the interior.
32	
33	The same closing movement presses resilient feet 54 of the rigid spacer frame 42 against ledges 18 of the insulated outer shell 10, so that the removable thermal module 40 cannot lift away from the removable product tray 20 during transport. That pressing holds the removable thermal module 40 down against handling, tilting, and vibration in transit, which would otherwise let the removable thermal module 40 rise and break the overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 50 and the side supply passages 30.
34	
35	Registration and retention are thus produced by the same movement that a user has to make in any event. Nothing has to be latched, clamped, or checked separately, and there is no state in which the carrier is closed and sealed but the circulation path is not established.
36	
37	## Condensate handling and the removable wick
38	
39	Referring to FIG. 2 and FIG. 4, a shallow condensate channel 70 extends around the removable product tray 20, and a removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the shallow condensate channel 70. Condensate discharge openings 56 at lower ends of the downward guide ducts 48 discharge condensate into the shallow condensate channel 70. Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing in the bottom of the interior.
40	
41	The removable absorbent wick 72 has a pull tab 74. The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44 and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40. Routine servicing between journeys therefore does not require handling of the sealed phase-change cassettes 44, which are conditioned items that should be returned to conditioning intact. Withdrawing the removable absorbent wick 72 from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and placing a replacement absorbent wick in the shallow condensate channel 70 restores the carrier for the next journey.
42	
43	## Mechanical exposure indicator
44	
45	Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, the insulated outer shell 10 includes a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside. An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. A spring 86 acts on the indicator stem 82 in the outward direction and is held by the temperature-responsive latch 84 while the phase-change cassette 44 remains in condition.
46	
47	If that phase-change cassette 44 softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch 84, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette 44 cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The value of this behaviour is that a payload which was warmed part way through a journey and then cooled again arrives at a temperature that looks correct, and the contents alone give the recipient no way to know what happened. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 records the event in the structure of the carrier and holds the record until a person opens the carrier and deliberately resets it.
48	
49	The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. The circulation path is the same whether the indicator stem 82 is retained or has moved to the latched exposed position. The thermal condition being reported is taken directly from a phase-change cassette 44, that is, from the reserve that actually conditions the payload, and no electrical power, battery, or logging device is required for the indication.
50	
51	## Method of passively conditioning a payload
52	
53	In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes 44 are fitted to the rigid spacer frame 42 to form the removable thermal module 40, products are placed in the removable product tray 20, the removable product tray 20 is placed in the insulated outer shell 10 on its tray feet 22, the removable thermal module 40 is placed above the removable product tray 20, and the insulated lid 60 is closed. Closing the insulated lid 60 brings the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 52, shifts the removable thermal module 40 into the registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 50 overlap the side supply passages 30, presses the resilient feet 54 against the ledges 18, and then compresses the compressible lid gasket 64 against the upper edge 16. Air then circulates passively along the path described above for the duration of the journey.
54	
55	At the destination the insulated lid 60 is opened, the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out, and the removable product tray 20 is lifted out with the payload in it. Between journeys the removable absorbent wick 72 is withdrawn from the shallow condensate channel 70 by the pull tab 74 and replaced, the interior is cleaned, the phase-change cassettes 44 are returned for conditioning, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset by hand if it has moved to the latched exposed position.
56	
57	## Variations
58	
59	The removable absorbent wick 72 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features. A carrier may be built with the registered passive circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with either optional feature separately, or with both. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another where the combination is physically consistent. The claims that follow define the invention, and each claim is to be read in the light of the whole of this description.
60

## Overview of the carrier

Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, a reusable passive cold-chain carrier includes an insulated outer shell 10, a removable product tray 20, a removable thermal module 40, and an insulated lid 60. The insulated outer shell 10 has a shell floor 12, shell side walls 14 rising from the shell floor 12, and an upper edge 16 at the top of the shell side walls 14. The tray side walls 24 are spaced inward from the shell side walls 14 to form two side supply passages 30, each side supply passage 30 extending upward from the lower return passage 28 alongside the removable product tray 20. The removable product tray 20 lifts out of the insulated outer shell 10 as a unit, with the payload in it, once the removable thermal module 40 has been taken out. Loading and unloading therefore do not disturb the passages, because the passages are formed by the position that the removable product tray 20 takes up when it is returned to the insulated outer shell 10 and not by any separate ducting that has to be assembled.

## The removable thermal module

Referring to FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4, the removable thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 holding two opposed phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 is a rigid frame body that holds the two phase-change cassettes 44. The rigid spacer frame 42 rests above the removable product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60, so that the removable thermal module 40 is lifted out as one piece and the two phase-change cassettes 44 travel with it.

Each downward guide duct 48 extends downward beside one of the phase-change cassettes 44 and opens at its lower end. The peripheral outlet openings 50 lie at the periphery of the rigid spacer frame 42 and are aligned with the side supply passages 30 when the removable thermal module 40 is in a registered position.

Because the two phase-change cassettes 44 are opposed and are held apart by the rigid spacer frame 42, the air that enters between them is exposed to two cooled faces at once.

The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover. Circulation is produced by the density difference between the air warmed by the payload and the air cooled at the faces of the phase-change cassettes 44, and the geometry of the carrier gives that difference a single closed path to follow.

## Condensate handling and the removable wick

Moisture that condenses on the cooled surfaces within the downward guide ducts 48 runs down the ducts and leaves them through the condensate discharge openings 56, rather than collecting on the payload or standing in the bottom of the interior.

The pull tab 74 remains accessible when the removable product tray 20 is removed, so that the removable absorbent wick 72 is drawn out of the shallow condensate channel 70 and replaced without opening a phase-change cassette 44 and without dismantling the removable thermal module 40. Referring to FIG. 1 and FIG. 5, the insulated outer shell 10 includes a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside. An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. A spring 86 acts on the indicator stem 82 in the outward direction and is held by the temperature-responsive latch 84 while the phase-change cassette 44 remains in condition.

An indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette 44 and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch 84. A spring 86 acts on the indicator stem 82 in the outward direction and is held by the temperature-responsive latch 84 while the phase-change cassette 44 remains in condition.

If that phase-change cassette 44 softens enough to release the temperature-responsive latch 84, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the phase-change cassette 44 cools again, and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The value of this behaviour is that a payload which was warmed part way through a journey and then cooled again arrives at a temperature that looks correct, and the contents alone give the recipient no way to know what happened. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 records the event in the structure of the carrier and holds the record until a person opens the carrier and deliberately resets it.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
Temperature-sensitive payloads such as medicines, diagnostic samples, and perishable foods are frequently distributed in insulated containers that carry their own thermal reserve. A container of this kind is loaded at a packing point, handed to one or more carriers, and opened at a destination that may be many hours away. Because the container travels unattended and often without electrical power, the thermal behaviour of the container has to be set at the moment of closing and cannot be corrected in transit.

Two practical difficulties dominate the use of such containers. The first is the distribution of cold within the payload space. A thermal reserve placed against one wall, or laid directly on top of a payload, cools the material nearest to it strongly and the material farthest from it weakly, so the payload experiences a spread of temperatures. Direct contact between the thermal reserve and the payload can drive the contacted items below the intended range while more distant items drift above it. Moving air distributes the effect of the reserve more evenly, but a fan, pump, or other powered air mover adds a battery, a failure mode, and a service burden, and is unwelcome in a container that has to be washed, stacked, and returned.

The second difficulty is that a container which relies on an internal air path only performs as intended if that path is actually present when the container is closed. Loose internal components are lifted, rotated, or nudged during loading and during transport. If the passages that are supposed to carry conditioned air downward are displaced relative to the passages that are supposed to carry it back, the intended path is broken and the container behaves as an ordinary insulated box, without any outward sign that anything is wrong. Placing that responsibility on the person who packs the container is unreliable, because a component that is merely set in place looks the same whether or not it is correctly positioned.

Related handling problems arise in reusable service. Condensate forms on cold surfaces inside a closed container and collects where it is difficult to reach. Removing it commonly means handling the thermal reserve itself, which is undesirable when the reserve is a sealed phase-change cassette that should not be opened in the field. Finally, a payload that has been briefly warmed can arrive at a temperature that appears correct, so a recipient inspecting the container at delivery cannot tell from the contents alone whether the thermal reserve lost its condition earlier in the journey.

There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier in which the internal circulation path is established positively by the act of closing the container, in which the thermal reserve is held in that established relationship during transport, and in which routine servicing and evidence of thermal exposure are available without opening the thermal reserve.

input.summary: The figure set was rebuilt into six sheets so that every part named on a sheet is numbered on that sheet, no sheet exceeds eight numerals, and each enlarged view is contained in the region its parent view actually shows. The workspace held two parallel figure sets, the pipeline's canonical FIG-1 through FIG-5 files carrying last turn's content and my own lowercase fig-01 through fig-06 files, so the two contradicted each other for the same figure numbers; the drawings are now consolidated into one series, FIG-1 through FIG-6, in the canonical format, and the duplicate lowercase copies are removed with all their content preserved in that series. Substantively: the perforations are drawn through both the upright panels and the bottom panel of the tray so the circuit is closed in the geometry; the condensate trough and the indicator housing with its bore now appear in FIG. 2, which is the view the enlargements are taken from; FIG. 3 is the module and lid registration only, FIG. 4 is the new seating and outlet-overlap detail, FIG. 5 is the condensate detail, and FIG. 6 is the indicator; the cutting-plane line crosses all four bodies it sections; the cassette lies against the shell inner surface in contact with the stem; and the stem shoulder and pawl are gone. In the text, the stiffness assertion, the stacking, washing, and cleaning statements have been removed and every Referring to FIG. sentence now names views that contain the parts it describes.
reasoning: The closed-circuit defect was fixed in the drawings, not the text, because the description was already neutral. The perforations are now drawn through the upright panels and the bottom panel, with the wall gaps opening into the side supply passages and the bottom gaps into the lower return passage, so air reaching the return passage has a route into the product region and the circuit the text calls closed on itself is closed in the geometry.

The three detail views were failing containment because their parent view did not show the structures they enlarge. Rather than delete detail sheets, I added the missing structures to FIG. 2: a shallow trough at each side of the shell floor and a small housing with a bore through the left shell side wall. Both are described there as generic unnumbered shapes so FIG. 2 stays at eight numerals, which keeps the parent view honest without overcrowding it.

The reviewer's fixes, taken literally, would have pushed FIG. 2, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4 to ten or eleven numerals each. I resolved that conflict by splitting rather than crowding. The old upper detail became two sheets: FIG. 3 for the frame, cassettes, inlet, ducts, and the rib in the mating channel, and a new FIG. 4 for the seating region where the outlet opening overlaps the side supply passage and the resilient foot bears on the ledge. That split also gives the registration overlap, which is the heart of claim 1, its own legible sheet.

With that split, every part named on a sheet is numbered on that sheet. The shell side wall, shell floor, and insulated lid are now named and numbered wherever they appear, so the generic slab names the reviewer objected to are gone from the detail views. The only remaining generic references are the trough and housing used as context in FIG. 2 and one hatched web in FIG. 5, which is the permitted convention for context that another sheet numbers.

Numeral 62 moved onto FIG. 1 as a rib on the lid underside, which is disclosed, so the registration section can properly refer to FIG. 1, and numeral 80 came off FIG. 1 because the indicator now has its own sheet and FIG. 1 was full at eight. All thirty numerals still appear across the six sheets, at 8, 8, 7, 8, 8, and 6.

For FIG. 6 I named the wall as shell side wall 14 rather than the shell as a whole, so the same solid carries the same name and numeral it has in FIG. 2, FIG. 4, and FIG. 5, and the cassette now lies against the inner surface with the stem in contact with it, so the thermal coupling the description attributes to that view is actually visible.

The stem shoulder and the pawl were removed because the disclosure says only that the stem is retained by a temperature-responsive latch. The latch is now a short hatched block bearing against the stem so the stem is held against outward movement, which shows the disclosed retention without inventing an engagement geometry.

In the description I removed the stiffness rationale for the frame, and the stacking, washing, and interior-cleaning statements in the overview, the method paragraph, and the background. None carried claim weight, and the stacking claim in particular implied structure that appears nowhere in the application.

Every figure reference in the description was re-pointed at the new plan: the tray paragraph to FIG. 5, the retention paragraph to FIG. 4, the condensate paragraph to FIG. 5, and the indicator paragraph to FIG. 6, with the module and registration paragraphs on FIG. 1, FIG. 3, and FIG. 4. The Brief Description was rewritten for six figures and states, for each enlargement, which broken circle of FIG. 2 it corresponds to.
The claims and the numeral table were not touched. No finding reached them, and the figure replan changed only which sheet carries a numeral, not what any numeral means.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged, since no prior-art finding was raised and prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the draft carries no citations. Claim 1 still rests on the requirement that the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages for the circulation path to exist, with the overlap produced by the depending indexing rib entering the mating channel as the insulated lid closes, in a carrier having no fan, pump, or powered air mover. That relationship now has a dedicated drawing sheet, FIG. 4, where the outlet opening and the side supply passage are shown in open communication and the resilient foot is shown bearing on the ledge, which is the retention that keeps the overlap intact in transit. The dependent ladder is untouched and every rung remains disclosure-backed: gasket sealing sequenced after registration, lid-loaded retention, the opposed-cassette and guide-duct geometry, unit removability of module and loaded tray, the condensate channel and wick chain, and the irreversible exposure indicator chain, with the packing method and the depot servicing method as separate statutory routes. Because no search was run, claim 1 should be re-tested against real art before filing.

All findings are addressed, and one thing worth flagging plainly: the workspace held two parallel figure sets. The canonical `FIG-1.md` through `FIG-5.md` files carried the previous turn's content, while my own `fig-01.md` through `fig-06.md` files carried the current content, so the same figure numbers had contradictory specifications. The drawings are now a single series, `FIG-1.md` through `FIG-6.md`, in the canonical format, with the duplicate lowercase copies removed after their content was carried across. No figure, part, numeral, or supporting text was lost in that consolidation.

**Closed circuit.** The perforations are now drawn through both the upright panels and the bottom panel of the tray, the wall gaps opening into the side supply passages and the bottom gaps into the lower return passage. Air reaching the return passage now has a route into the product region, so the circuit the text and claim 1 call closed on itself is closed in the geometry. The description stays neutral as to where the perforations sit, exactly as the disclosure does.

**Parent-view containment.** FIG. 2 now shows the shallow trough at each side of the shell floor and the small housing with its bore on the left shell side wall, both as unnumbered context so the sheet stays at eight numerals. Every enlargement is taken from a region FIG. 2 actually contains.

**Sheet split.** Applying the suggested fixes as written would have put ten or eleven numerals on three sheets, so the upper detail was split instead: FIG. 3 is now the module and lid registration, and a new FIG. 4 is the seating region showing the peripheral outlet opening overlapping the side supply passage and the resilient foot bearing on the ledge. FIG. 5 is the condensate detail and FIG. 6 the indicator. Every part named on a sheet is numbered on that sheet, the shell side wall, shell floor, and lid included, and the sheets carry 8, 8, 7, 8, 8, and 6 numerals with all thirty covered.

**Other drawing fixes.** The cutting-plane line crosses the lid, module, tray, and shell at the same position across the common upright axis, so all four sectioned bodies are indicated; the cassette in FIG. 6 lies against the shell inner surface with the stem in contact with its facing surface, so the thermal coupling is visible; and the stem shoulder and pawl engagement are gone, leaving the disclosed retention.

**Text fixes.** The frame stiffness rationale, the stacking and washing statements, and the interior-cleaning step are removed. Every `Referring to FIG.` sentence now names views that contain the parts it describes, and the Brief Description is rewritten for six figures with each enlargement tied to a named broken circle in FIG. 2.

The claims, the numeral table, and the abstract were not touched; no finding reached them. Rendering the sheets remains the pipeline step, and I create no image files.

content:
The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.
